entries.translit: kol-ʾaḇnê mizbēaḥ kᵉ-ʾaḇnê-ḡir mᵉnuppāṣôṯ lō-yāqumû ʾăšērîm wᵉ-ḥammānîm
entries.strongs: H842 (ʾăšērāh, pl. ʾăšērîm); H2553 (ḥammān 'sun-pillar, incense-altar'); H4196 (mizbēaḥ 'altar'); H1615 (gir 'chalk, lime'); H5310 (nāp̄aṣ 'shatter')
entries.lemma: the cult-purge inventory of 27:9 — the altar-stones 'like crushed chalkstones' + ʾăšērîm 'Asherim' (the wooden poles of the goddess Asherah) + ḥammānîm 'sun-pillars'
entries.literal: all the stones of the altar like chalkstones shattered; Asherim and sun-pillars shall not stand
entries.standardEnglish: all the stones of the altar as chalkstones that are beaten in sunder, so that the Asherim and the sun-images shall rise no more (ASV); no Asherim or sun-images shall stand (JPS)
entries.wohChoice: 'when he makes all the altar-stones like crushed chalkstones, no Asherim or sun-pillars shall stand' — ʾăšērîm transliterated 'Asherim' (the wooden cult-poles; the goddess Asherah / Ugaritic ʾAṯiratu link carried in commentary, the central athirat-asherah entry deliberately NOT applied — the referent is the cult-object, not the goddess); ḥammānîm 'sun-pillars' (with NJPS 'incense-altars' noted). The kpr 'atoned for' of the same verse is governed by the overlay kupar-atonement-isaiah (appliesTo extended to ISA-27:9); ʿăwōn 'iniquity' by the central avon-iniquity-cross-corpus-keyword (extended to ISA-27:9).
entries.rationale: The condition of the atonement of 27:9 is the demolition of the cult: 'when he makes all the altar-stones (ʾaḇnê mizbēaḥ) like crushed chalkstones (kᵉ-ʾaḇnê-ḡir mᵉnuppāṣôṯ; gir 'chalk, lime', nāp̄aṣ 'shatter'), Asherim and sun-pillars shall not stand.' Two lexical decisions. (i) ʾăšērîm (H842) are the wooden cult-poles of the goddess Asherah — the Hebrew reflex, by the regular ṯ->š shift, of Ugaritic ʾAṯiratu (ʾaṯrt), ʾIlu's consort and mother of the gods (central athirat-asherah-mother-goddess-cross-corpus-ugaritic-hebrew-bible). The translation transliterates 'Asherim' (with 'Asherah-poles / sacred poles' as equivalents), the standard rendering; the central athirat-asherah entry is deliberately NOT applied to ISA-27:9, because its wohChoice is the Ugaritic goddess proper-name 'ʾAṯiratu' and the referent at 27:9 is the cult-OBJECT (the pole being demolished), not the goddess herself — a referent/rendering mismatch of the same kind that governs the yamm (deified Sea vs common-noun sea) and rephaim (giants vs shades) non-extensions. The goddess/pole cross-corpus link is documented here and in commentary, not asserted by an appliesTo extension. (ii) ḥammānîm (H2553) are rendered 'sun-pillars / sun-images' (the standard value, the cultic stelae associated with sun-worship), with the NJPS 'incense-altars' noted as the live alternative. The renderings are standard and carry no lens (Wildberger, Isaiah 13-27; Blenkinsopp, Isaiah 1-39; BDB, HALOT s.v. ʾăšērāh, ḥammān).

entries.source: עִיר בְּצוּרָה בָּדָד … כִּי לֹא עַם־בִּינוֹת הוּא … עֹשֵׂהוּ … וְיֹצְרוֹ
entries.translit: ʿîr bᵉṣûrāh bāḏāḏ … kî lō ʿam-bînôṯ hû … ʿōśēhû … wᵉ-yōṣᵉrô
entries.strongs: H5892 (ʿîr 'city'); H1219 (bāṣar 'fortify'); H909 (bāḏāḏ 'alone, solitary'); H998 (bînāh 'understanding'); H6213 (ʿāśāh 'make'); H3335 (yāṣar 'form, fashion')
entries.lemma: the unnamed ʿîr bᵉṣûrāh 'fortified city' left solitary (27:10) + the withered harvest, the ʿam-bînôṯ 'people without understanding', and its ʿōśēhû 'Maker' / yōṣᵉrô 'Fashioner' (27:11)
entries.partOfSpeech: noun-phrase (unnamed city) + verbal clauses + two divine-epithet participles
entries.literal: for the fortified city is solitary … for it is not a people of understanding; therefore its Maker will not pity it, and its Fashioner will not favor it
entries.standardEnglish: For the fortified city is solitary … it is a people of no understanding; therefore he that made them will not have compassion upon them, and he that formed them will show them no favor (ASV/JPS)
entries.wohChoice: 'the fortified city is solitary … it is a people without understanding; therefore its Maker will not have compassion on it, and its Fashioner will not be gracious to it' — the city left UNNAMED, its referent (a foreign / enemy capital vs Jerusalem itself under judgment) unresolved in the line and weighed only in commentary; ʿōśēhû / yōṣᵉrô 'its Maker' / 'its Fashioner' (the creation-verbs ʿśh 'make' and yṣr 'form, fashion').
entries.rationale: 27:10-11 describe an unnamed ʿîr bᵉṣûrāh 'fortified city' (bāṣar 'cut off, make inaccessible, fortify') left bāḏāḏ 'solitary, alone', a forsaken pasture where the calf grazes and strips the branches (27:10); when its harvest (qāṣîr) dries up the boughs are broken and women come to kindle them, 'for it is a people without understanding (ʿam-bînôṯ), therefore its Maker (ʿōśēhû, ʿśh) will not have compassion on it and its Fashioner (yōṣᵉrô, yṣr) will not be gracious to it' (27:11). The renderings are standard; the one flagged point is that the city is deliberately left UNNAMED, and its referent is a scholarly crux — a foreign or enemy capital (a Samaria-, Moab-, or generic-oppressor city, the counterpart to the strong city of salvation in 26:1) versus Jerusalem itself under judgment. The translation renders the city plainly and does not resolve the identification in the line, leaving it for commentary (accuracy-before-lens). ʿōśēhû 'its Maker' and yōṣᵉrô 'its Fashioner' are the two creation-participles applied to the people; they are rendered by their standard values and receive no lens. The renderings are standard (Wildberger, Isaiah 13-27; Blenkinsopp, Isaiah 1-39; Kaiser, Isaiah 13-39, OTL).

entries.source: יַחְבֹּט יְהוָה מִשִּׁבֹּלֶת הַנָּהָר עַד־נַחַל מִצְרָיִם וְאַתֶּם תְּלֻקְּטוּ לְאַחַד אֶחָד
entries.translit: yaḥbōṭ YHWH miš-šibbōleṯ han-nāhār ʿaḏ-naḥal miṣrāyim wᵉ-ʾattem tᵉluqqᵉṭû lᵉ-ʾaḥaḏ ʾeḥāḏ
entries.strongs: H2251 (ḥāḇaṭ 'beat off, thresh'); H7641 (šibbōleṯ 'ear of grain; flowing stream'); H5104 (nāhār 'river'); H5158 (naḥal 'wadi, brook'); H3950 (lāqaṭ 'glean, gather up')
entries.lemma: yaḥbōṭ 'beat off / thresh' (unexpressed object) + the šibbōleṯ 'flowing stream' / 'ear of grain' pun + han-nāhār 'the River' (Euphrates) / naḥal miṣrayim 'the Wadi of Egypt' (the idealized N-S boundaries) + tᵉluqqᵉṭû lᵉ-ʾaḥaḏ ʾeḥāḏ 'gathered one by one'
entries.literal: YHWH will beat off from the flowing stream of the River to the Wadi of Egypt, and you shall be gleaned one by one
entries.standardEnglish: Jehovah will beat off his fruit from the flood of the River unto the brook of Egypt; and ye shall be gathered one by one (ASV); the LORD will beat off [His fruit] from the flood of the River unto the Brook of Egypt (JPS)
entries.wohChoice: 'YHWH will beat off the grain, from the flowing stream of the River to the Wadi of Egypt, and you shall be gathered up one by one' — the unexpressed object of yaḥbōṭ supplied as 'the grain' (JPS supplies '[His fruit]'); šibbōleṯ 'flowing stream' (with the 'ear of grain' pun on the threshing-verb flagged); han-nāhār = the Euphrates, naḥal miṣrayim = the Wadi of Egypt (the southern boundary); tᵉluqqᵉṭû lᵉ-ʾaḥaḏ ʾeḥāḏ 'gathered up one by one', the eschatological ingathering.
entries.rationale: 27:12 opens the ingathering. yaḥbōṭ (ḥbṭ 'beat off, thresh', as one beats olives or grain from the tree or stalk, cf. Deut 24:20; Ruth 2:17) has an unexpressed object; the translation supplies 'the grain' (JPS supplies '[His fruit]'), and the verb governs the harvest-imagery of the whole verse. šibbōleṯ ha-nāhār is a deliberate pun: šibbōleṯ means both 'flowing stream, channel, flood' (so 'the flowing stream of the River', JPS 'the flood of the River') AND 'ear of grain', resonating with the threshing-verb — the translation renders 'flowing stream' and flags the grain-pun. han-nāhār 'the River' is the Euphrates and naḥal miṣrayim 'the Wadi of Egypt' (Wadi el-ʿArish) is the southern boundary — together the idealized north-south extent of the land from which Israel is gathered. tᵉluqqᵉṭû (lqṭ 'glean, gather up') lᵉ-ʾaḥaḏ ʾeḥāḏ 'you shall be gathered up one by one' completes the harvest-and-gleaning image of the eschatological gathering of Israel. The renderings are standard and carry no lens; the entry records the supplied object, the šibbōleṯ pun, and the boundary-toponyms (Wildberger, Isaiah 13-27; Blenkinsopp, Isaiah 1-39; BDB, HALOT s.v. šibbōleṯ).

entries.source: יִתָּקַע בְּשׁוֹפָר גָּדוֹל וּבָאוּ הָאֹבְדִים בְּאֶרֶץ אַשּׁוּר וְהַנִּדָּחִים בְּאֶרֶץ מִצְרָיִם וְהִשְׁתַּחֲווּ לַיהוָה
entries.translit: yittāqaʿ bᵉ-šôp̄ār gāḏôl û-ḇāʾû hā-ʾōḇᵉḏîm bᵉ-ʾereṣ ʾaššûr wᵉ-han-niddāḥîm bᵉ-ʾereṣ miṣrāyim wᵉ-hištaḥăwû la-YHWH
entries.strongs: H8628 (tāqaʿ 'blow, thrust'); H7782 (šôp̄ār 'ram's-horn, trumpet'); H6 (ʾāḇaḏ 'perish, be lost'); H5080 (nāḏaḥ 'drive away, banish'); H7812 (šāḥāh / ḥwh 'bow down, do obeisance, worship')
entries.lemma: šôp̄ār gāḏôl 'a great trumpet' (blown, Niphal yittāqaʿ) + hā-ʾōḇᵉḏîm 'those perishing / the lost' (in Assyria) / han-niddāḥîm 'the driven-out / outcast' (in Egypt) + hištaḥăwû 'they shall bow down' (cultic worship of YHWH)
entries.partOfSpeech: noun (trumpet) + two substantival participles (the lost / the outcast) + verb (worship)
entries.literal: a great trumpet shall be blown, and those perishing in the land of Assyria and those driven out in the land of Egypt shall come, and they shall bow down to YHWH
entries.standardEnglish: a great trumpet shall be blown; and they shall come that were ready to perish in the land of Assyria, and they that were outcasts in the land of Egypt; and they shall worship Jehovah (ASV); a great horn shall be blown (JPS)
entries.wohChoice: 'a great trumpet shall be blown, and those perishing in the land of Assyria and those driven out in the land of Egypt shall come, and they shall bow down to YHWH on the holy mountain in Jerusalem' — šôp̄ār 'trumpet' (the ram's-horn; JPS 'horn'; the transliteration 'shofar' marks the cultic register); hā-ʾōḇᵉḏîm 'those perishing / the lost', han-niddāḥîm 'those driven out / the outcast'; hištaḥăwû 'bow down' in the cultic-worship register of YHWH — the central hishtachavah-bow-down-obeisance-worship entry (wohChoice 'made obeisance', the human-homage register) deliberately NOT applied. The eschatological ingathering carried in commentary.
entries.rationale: The chapter's climax: yittāqaʿ bᵉ-šôp̄ār gāḏôl 'a great trumpet shall be blown' (yittāqaʿ, Niphal of tqʿ 'blow'; šôp̄ār, the ram's-horn) summons hā-ʾōḇᵉḏîm 'those perishing / the lost ones' (ʾbd) in the land of Assyria and han-niddāḥîm 'the driven-out / outcast / dispersed' (ndḥ) in the land of Egypt to come and hištaḥăwû 'bow down' to YHWH on the holy mountain (har ha-qōḏeš) at Jerusalem. Four decisions, all standard. (i) šôp̄ār gāḏôl is 'a great trumpet' (the ram's-horn; JPS 'a great horn'; the transliteration 'shofar' is noted for the cultic register); no central or overlay šôp̄ār entry previously existed. (ii) hā-ʾōḇᵉḏîm 'those perishing / the lost' and han-niddāḥîm 'those driven out / the outcast / dispersed' are the two groups of exiles, rendered by their standard values. (iii) hištaḥăwû (Hishtaphel of ḥwh, H7812) is here cultic worship of the deity — 'bow down / worship' YHWH — a different register from the human-homage 'made obeisance' of the central hishtachavah-bow-down-obeisance-worship entry (scoped to the Genesis Yosef-cycle, wohChoice 'made obeisance'); that entry is deliberately NOT applied to ISA-27:13, since the referent here is worship of YHWH, not homage to a human superior — a register mismatch of the kind recorded for the elohim, refaim, and yamm non-extensions. The translation renders 'bow down' (with 'worship' as the cultic equivalent). (iv) the toponyms Aššûr (Assyria), Miṣrayim (Egypt), and Yᵉrûšālāim (Jerusalem) are standard. The great-trumpet ingathering of the lost and the outcast is the eschatological gathering-of-the-dispersed, developed in commentary (cf. Matt 24:31); the renderings are standard and carry no lens (Wildberger, Isaiah 13-27; Blenkinsopp, Isaiah 1-39; BDB, HALOT s.v. šôp̄ār, nāḏaḥ).

entries.lemma: bārāʾ I 'create' (Qal and Niphal; the subject is always the God of Israel)
entries.partOfSpeech: verb (Qal perfect, imperfect and participle; Niphal perfect)
entries.literal: create
entries.standardEnglish: create; Creator (ASV, NRSV, NJPS)
entries.wohChoice: 'create' / 'Creator' throughout Isaiah (40:26, 28; 42:5; 43:1, 7, 15; 45:7, 8, 12, 18; 48:7; 54:16; 65:17, 18). The central `bara` entry ('shape', claim_type inferred, appliesTo Gen 1:1, 21, 27) is deliberately NOT extended to Isaiah. yāṣar stays 'form' (central `yatsar`) and ʿāśāh stays 'make' (central `asah`), so the three verbs remain distinct in English: 'created ... formed ... made' (43:7; 45:18).
entries.rationale: The central `bara` entry renders bārāʾ 'shape' on the strength of Gen 1, where it sets the verb apart from ʿāśāh and yāṣar. The Translator's draft extended that rendering to Second and Third Isaiah, and the Editor declines the extension for four reasons. (1) Range of objects: in Isaiah bārāʾ governs darkness and calamity (45:7), righteousness and salvation (45:8), the 'new things' of history (48:7), the smith and the destroyer (54:16), and Jerusalem 'as a rejoicing' (65:18). English 'shape' implies a material being worked, which is not how these objects behave. The lexica (BDB, HALOT s.v. בָּרָא I; Bernhardt, TDOT 2:245-248; Schmidt, THAT 1:336-339) and the commentators who study the Isaiah usage (Stuhlmueller, Creative Redemption in Deutero-Isaiah, 1970; Westermann, Isaiah 40-66, OTL 1969; Blenkinsopp, Isaiah 40-55, AB 19A, 2002) agree that the verb names the sovereign, effortless bringing-about of something new, with no material and no tool. (2) The lexical point the central entry wants to make is better served by 'create'. In Isaiah, bārāʾ is set in parallel with yāṣar, the potter's verb (43:1, 7; 45:7, 18), and English 'shape' and 'form' are near-synonyms of the same craft register, so the contrast the Hebrew draws between the two verbs would disappear. (3) Lens risk: 'shaping new skies' or 'shaping humankind' reads as manufacture, which suggests a craft-and-workshop reading that the Hebrew of these verses does not support. Rule 1 (accuracy above lens) excludes a rendering that leans toward a project reading without a lexical basis. (4) The ex nihilo debate is not settled by the English 'create': the word leaves open whether Second Isaiah teaches creation from nothing (the majority of commentators, Westermann included, think the text does not raise the question), so the rendering is neutral where the Hebrew is neutral. The canon itself quotes Isa 43:7 as 'créés, formés et faits' ('created, formed and made'), so the standard triad is also the wording the reception text uses. Whether the Genesis 'shape' decision should be revisited in the light of the Isaiah usage is outside this pass and is flagged to the founder in wave-i2-editor-report.md. Wave I-1 extension: ûḇārāʾ YHWH at 4:5 'and YHWH will create' (over Mount Zion a cloud, smoke and fire), the same 'create'; the LXX's kai hēxei ('and he will come', as if ûḇāʾ) is reported in commentary and not adopted.

entries.strongs: H430 (ʾĕlōhîm); H410 (ʾēl); H433 (ʾĕlôah)
entries.lemma: the three Hebrew words for 'god / God' in Isaiah's incomparability and denial formulas
entries.literal: God / a god
entries.standardEnglish: God / a god (ASV, NRSV, NJPS)
entries.wohChoice: 'God' wherever ʾĕlōhîm, ʾēl or ʾĕlôah designates YHWH or is the term whose existence the denial formula rules out ('besides me there is no God', 44:6; 45:5, 14, 21; 'Is there a God besides me?', 44:8; 'he is God', 45:18; 'I am God', 43:12; 45:22; 'To whom will you liken God?', 40:18; 'Thus says God, YHWH', 42:5; 'a God who hides himself', 45:15; 'as when God overthrew Sodom', 13:19). Lower-case 'god / a god / gods' where the word denotes a made idol (42:17; 44:10, 15, 17; 45:20) and at 43:10 ('before me no god was formed'), where the verb nôṣar puts the noun in the vocabulary of idol-manufacture. The central 'the Elohim' convention (`elohim-as-translation`, scoped to Genesis 1) and the transliterations 'El' (central El-compound entries) and 'Eloah' (central `shaddai-eloah`, scoped to Job) are NOT applied in Isaiah.
entries.rationale: The Isaiah overlay has rendered suffixed and construct ʾĕlōhîm 'God' since chapter 24 (`elohei-yisrael-god-of-israel-isaiah-24`, `elohai-elohenu-doxology-isaiah-25`, `elohim-as-god-observers-53-4-isaiah`). This entry extends the same practice to the absolute, articular and indefinite forms and to the synonyms ʾēl and ʾĕlôah, which Second Isaiah uses interchangeably in one formula. In 44:6-8 the three words alternate inside a single speech ('there is no ʾĕlōhîm', 44:6; 'is there an ʾĕlôah besides me?', 44:8; cf. ʾēl, 45:21-22). Transliterating one of them ('Eloah') while translating the others would mark a distinction the text does not draw, so the central `shaddai-eloah` entry, whose rationale concerns the Aramean-Wisdom divine-name register of Job, is applied in Isaiah only to Shaddai at 13:6 (a name, kept by NJPS and carrying the šōḏ/šadday pun) and not to ʾĕlôah at 44:8. The capitalization follows ASV and NRSV: 'God' for the deity whom the formulas identify with YHWH, and 'a god / gods' for the idol made by human hands, the object of the polemic in 44:9-20 and 45:20 (Westermann, Isaiah 40-66, 1969; Blenkinsopp, Isaiah 40-55, AB 19A, 2002). The articular predicate hûʾ hā-ʾĕlōhîm 'he is God' at 45:18 belongs to the Deuteronomic identification formula (Deut 4:35, 39; 1 Kgs 18:39) and is rendered 'God' under this book-level practice. The corpus renders the same formula 'YHWH, he is the Elohim' at 1 Kgs 18:39 (1-kings-woh), and that cross-corpus divergence is flagged to the founder in wave-i2-editor-report.md rather than settled in this overlay. Wave I-3 (Isa 8): 'God' for ʾēl in the clause kî ʿimmānû ʾēl (8:10) and for suffixed ʾĕlōhāyw at 8:19 and 8:21 on the construal of ASV and KJV, in which the prophet replies and the word designates the God of Israel. JPS 1917 prints 'their God' but keeps 8:19b-20a inside the advisers' quotation, so it does not support that punctuation. The alternative construal of 8:19, the continued quotation (JPS 1917, NJPS) with ʾĕlōhîm as the dead (NJPS 'its divine beings', with the note 'the shades of the dead', cf. 1 Sam 28:13), would make 8:19 and 8:21 lower-case instances under the entry's own rule for non-YHWH referents; it is reported in commentary, and the ASV construal is kept in the line (founder ruling 2026-11-26). Wave I-3 extension: ʾēl in ʾēl gibbôr at 10:21 is 'God' (YHWH), here inside the capitalised title 'the Mighty God' governed by el-gibbor-mighty-god-isaiah.

entries.translit: rûaḥ (rûaḥ YHWH; rûḥî 'my rûaḥ'; rûḥô 'his rûaḥ'; rûaḥ mim-mārôm)
entries.lemma: rûaḥ 'wind, breath, spirit', here as YHWH's endowing or outpoured rûaḥ
entries.literal: breath / wind / spirit
entries.standardEnglish: the Spirit / my Spirit (ASV); spirit / my spirit (NRSV, NJPS)
entries.wohChoice: lower-case 'spirit' for YHWH's rûaḥ in the endowment and outpouring passages: 'a spirit from on high' (32:15), 'the spirit of YHWH' (40:13), 'my spirit' (42:1; 44:3), 'and his spirit' (48:16). 'breath' where rûaḥ YHWH blows on the grass (40:7), and 'spirit' for the human rûaḥ given 'to those who walk in it' (42:5, parallel to nᵉšāmāh 'breath'). No capital 'Spirit'. The Kings/Ezekiel transliteration 'ruach' (overlay entries `ruach-yhwh-and-prophetic-ruach-transliteration-kings`, `ruach-agent-gift-and-side-ezekiel`) is not adopted in Isaiah.
entries.rationale: The ASV capital 'Spirit' carries the later Christian reading of rûaḥ as a person of the Trinity, which the Hebrew does not mark. The modern scholarly translations (NRSV, NJPS) and the commentaries (Westermann, Isaiah 40-66; Blenkinsopp, Isaiah 40-55, AB 19A; Wildberger, Isaiah 28-39) print lower-case 'spirit' in these verses, and the Editor follows them. The indefinite rûaḥ mim-mārôm at 32:15 has no article and is kept indefinite, 'a spirit from on high'. Transliteration was considered and declined. In Kings and Ezekiel the corpus keeps 'ruach' where the rûaḥ acts in narrative as an agent that lifts, carries or sets a prophet on his feet, and the wind/spirit ambiguity carries the story (2 Kgs 2:16; Ezek 3:12-14). In Isaiah's poetry the rûaḥ is endowed or poured out in parallel with water and blessing (32:15; 44:3) or set upon a servant (42:1), and English 'spirit' gives that sense without loss. One consequence should be named: Ezekiel's own outpouring and endowment verses (Ezek 37:14; 39:29; overlay `ruach-agent-gift-and-side-ezekiel`) use 'ruach', so Isa 44:3 'I will pour my spirit' and Ezek 39:29 'I have poured out my ruach' now differ in English. That cross-corpus question is flagged to the founder in wave-i2-editor-report.md. The 40:7 / 40:13 sequence ('the breath of YHWH' blows; 'who has directed the spirit of YHWH?') is the same construct rûaḥ YHWH in two senses, and the commentary at 40:13 points this out. Wave I-1 extension: at 4:4 rûaḥ is the agent of YHWH's purge, bᵉrûaḥ mišpāṭ û-ḇᵉrûaḥ bāʿēr 'by a spirit of justice and by a spirit of burning' (ASV, NRSV), and the same lower-case 'spirit' is used; NJPS likewise has 'a spirit of judgment … a spirit of purging', and the wind sense of rûaḥ (HALOT) is recorded in commentary. Wave I-3 extension: at 11:2 the four occurrences of rûaḥ ('the spirit of YHWH shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding …') are all lower case, with NJPS (checked) against ASV, which capitalises only the first. Two other rûaḥ sites in the chapter lie outside this entry and take the standard English without an entry: 11:4 rûaḥ śᵉp̄āṯāyw 'the breath of his lips' (the king's own breath; ASV, JPS 1917, NJPS) and 11:15 baʿyām rûḥô 'with his scorching wind' (YHWH's wind over the River; ASV, NJPS 'wind'). No wohChoice change is proposed; if a later wave wants the entry to govern every rûaḥ of YHWH, a 'wind' clause for 11:15 would be a wohChoice modification (major bump).

entries.lemma: tōhû 'formlessness, waste, emptiness, nothingness'
entries.literal: waste / emptiness
entries.standardEnglish: vanity, a thing of nought, a waste, in vain (ASV); nothing, emptiness, chaos, in vain (NRSV)
entries.wohChoice: context decides: 'emptiness' where tōhû means worthlessness or nothingness (29:21; 40:17, 23; 44:9); 'in vain' for the adverbial idiom 'seek me tōhû' (45:19); 'a wasteland' at 45:18 ('he did not create it a wasteland, he formed it to be inhabited'), where tōhû is the uninhabitable land opposed to lā-šeḇeṯ 'to be inhabited' and echoes the Gen 1:2 pair rendered 'wasteland and emptiness' by the central `tohu-vavohu` entry. The 'chaos' of `qiryat-tohu-city-of-chaos-isaiah-24` stays at 24:10 only.
entries.rationale: BDB and HALOT give tōhû a range running from concrete 'desert, waste' to abstract 'emptiness, nothingness', and Second Isaiah uses both ends. In the polemic against the nations and the idols (40:17, 23; 44:9) and in the forensic idiom of 29:21 ('turn aside the righteous with tōhû', i.e. with empty pleas), the sense is worthlessness, and 'emptiness' keeps one English word across those sites. At 45:18 the noun stands in a creation formula opposite 'to be inhabited', and the concrete sense applies: the earth was not made an uninhabitable waste (ASV and NJPS 'a waste'; Blenkinsopp, AB 19A, 'a formless waste'; Westermann). 'A wasteland' is chosen to match the corpus's Gen 1:2 rendering ('wasteland and emptiness', central `tohu-vavohu`), since 45:18 is a deliberate allusion to that verse, and the echo should stay visible in English. The Translator's 'as chaos' (extending the 24:10 overlay entry) is declined: 'chaos' is defensible (NRSV) but brings in the mythic chaos-battle register that the antithesis with 'inhabited' does not call for. At 45:19 'Seek me tōhû' is the adverbial 'in vain' of all the standard versions.

entries.lemma: yôṣēr, the Qal participle of yāṣar 'form', used substantively as 'potter'
entries.partOfSpeech: participle (substantive with article; suffixed verbal participle)
entries.literal: the former / the potter; the one who formed him/it
entries.standardEnglish: the potter; his Maker / him that fashioneth it (ASV); the potter (NRSV at 45:9)
entries.wohChoice: 'the potter' for the free-standing substantive with the article (hay-yôṣēr, 29:16), where the craftsman is named as such; 'the one who formed him / the one who forms it' for the suffixed participle yōṣᵉrô with God as subject (29:16b; 45:9 twice; 45:11), under the central `yatsar` entry ('form'), so the potter's verb stays visible and the clay image is carried by 'clay' and 'formed'.
entries.rationale: yāṣar is the potter's verb, and its participle yôṣēr is the ordinary word for 'potter' (Jer 18:2-6; BDB, HALOT). Isaiah exploits the double sense in its clay passages (29:16; 45:9; 64:7). One ruling covers the book: where the participle stands as a free substantive with the article and names the craftsman over against the clay ('Shall the potter be regarded as the clay?', 29:16), the line says 'the potter', as ASV, NRSV and NJPS do. Where the participle carries a pronominal suffix and refers to God as someone's maker, the line keeps the verbal force, 'the one who formed him', so the Hebrew link to 43:1, 44:2, 24 ('who formed you') is not broken by a title such as 'his Maker'. This is the more literal option and the one that keeps the yāṣar / bārāʾ / ʿāśāh distinction visible; NRSV's 'the potter' at 45:9b is recorded in commentary as the idiomatic alternative. The same rule will govern Isa 64:7 when that chapter is translated.

entries.lemma: tôrāh 'instruction, teaching, direction; law'
entries.literal: instruction / teaching
entries.standardEnglish: law (ASV); teaching (NRSV at 42:4, 21; NJPS throughout)
entries.wohChoice: 'teaching' in Isaiah: 'the coastlands wait for his teaching' (42:4); 'to magnify teaching and make it glorious' (42:21); 'whose teaching they did not obey' (42:24); consistent with the plural 'the teachings' already ratified at 24:5 (`chanef-broken-everlasting-covenant-isaiah-24`).
entries.rationale: tôrāh derives from the Hiphil of yrh 'point, direct, instruct', and in the prophets it often means the instruction a priest, prophet or teacher gives, not a written law-code (BDB; HALOT; García López, TDOT 15:609-646; Jensen, The Use of tôrâ by Isaiah, CBQMS 3, 1973). Isaiah's own usage leans to that sense: 'the tôrāh of our God' parallels 'the word of YHWH' (1:10), tôrāh goes out from Zion to the nations (2:3), and the prophet's disciples hold it sealed (8:16, 20). NJPS renders 'teaching' throughout, NRSV has 'teaching' at 42:4 and 42:21, and Blenkinsopp (AB 19A) and Westermann read 42:4 as instruction carried to the coastlands. The overlay already rendered the plural tôrôṯ 'the teachings' at 24:5, so 'teaching' also keeps the book consistent. At 42:24 the sense comes nearer to covenant law ('whose tôrāh they did not obey'); 'teaching' still fits, and NRSV's 'law' there is recorded in commentary. The claim is inferred rather than direct because ASV and the traditional English have 'law'.

entries.source: הֵילֵל בֶּן־שָׁחַר · כּוֹכְבֵי־אֵל · הַר־מוֹעֵד · יַרְכְּתֵי צָפוֹן · עֶלְיוֹן
entries.translit: hêlēl ben-šāḥar; kôḵᵉḇê-ʾēl; har-môʿēḏ; yarkᵉṯê ṣāp̄ôn; ʿelyôn
entries.strongs: H1966 (hêlēl); H7837 (šaḥar); H3556 + H410 (kôḵāḇ, ʾēl); H2022 + H4150 (har, môʿēḏ); H3411 + H6828 (yᵉrēḵāh, ṣāp̄ôn); H5945 (ʿelyôn)
entries.lemma: the mythic vocabulary of the taunt over the king of Babylon, Isa 14:12-15
entries.partOfSpeech: noun phrases (vocative epithet; construct chains; divine title)
entries.literal: shining one, son of dawn; stars of El/God; mount of meeting; recesses of Zaphon/the north; Most High
entries.standardEnglish: day-star, son of the morning; the stars of God; the mount of congregation; the uttermost parts of the north; the Most High (ASV) · Day Star, son of Dawn; the stars of God; the mount of assembly; the heights of Zaphon; the Most High (NRSV)
entries.wohChoice: 'O day star, son of the dawn' (common nouns, no capital, no 'Lucifer'); 'the stars of God'; 'the mount of assembly'; 'in the far reaches of Zaphon' (ṣāp̄ôn as the divine mountain's name, with NRSV/NJPS), and yarkᵉṯê kept as 'the far reaches' in both v13 and v15 ('the far reaches of the pit') so the height/depth mirror stays visible; ʿelyôn 'the Most High'. The šāmayim of vv12-13 is 'the heavens' (divine-realm register of the central `shamayim` entry).
entries.rationale: The taunt borrows the language of a West-Semitic myth of a star-deity who tried to climb to the throne on the divine mountain and was thrown down. The usual comparandum is ʿAṯtaru, who takes Baʿlu's throne on Ṣapunu and comes down again (KTU 1.6 i 53-65; Craigie, ZAW 85, 1973; Day, Yahweh and the Gods and Goddesses of Canaan, 2000; Wildberger, Isaiah 13-27, 1997). The translation keeps the vocabulary of that myth readable without turning the line into a myth of its own. hêlēl (√hll 'shine') is rendered 'day star' with ASV and NRSV; capitalized proper names ('Helel son of Shahar') would claim more than the Hebrew settles. The Vulgate's lucifer, the source of the later 'Lucifer' reading, belongs to the reception history and is given in commentary. ṣāp̄ôn is given as the mountain's name, 'Zaphon', with NRSV and NJPS and the consensus of the commentators (Clifford, The Cosmic Mountain, 1972; Day; Blenkinsopp, AB 19), because 'mount of assembly' and the stars of ʾēl set the scene on the divine mountain, not at a compass point. This follows the central `mount-sapunu-tsafon-cosmic-mountain-cross-corpus-ugaritic-hebrew-bible` entry's instruction to render the Hebrew cognate conventionally. kôḵᵉḇê-ʾēl and ʿelyôn keep the book's 'God' and the standard 'the Most High'. The central El-compound entries (`el-elyon`) transliterate only inside compounds, and the 'stars of El' reading cited in the central `kokhvei-boqer` rationale is recorded in commentary, not imposed on the line.

entries.strongs: H7965 (šālôm); H7451 (raʿ)
entries.lemma: the antithetic pair šālôm / rāʿ in the creation-hymn participles of 45:7
entries.literal: who makes well-being and creates harm
entries.standardEnglish: I make peace, and create evil (ASV, KJV); I make weal and create woe (NRSV); I make weal and create woe (NJPS)
entries.wohChoice: 'who forms light and creates darkness, who makes well-being and creates calamity': šālôm 'well-being' and rāʿ 'calamity', the non-moral pair that the antithesis requires.
entries.rationale: rāʿ covers moral evil and physical harm alike (BDB, HALOT s.v. רַע). In 45:7 it stands opposite šālôm, which here means welfare or prosperity, not the absence of war. The four participles form two pairs of opposites (light / darkness; well-being / harm) that sum up everything YHWH does, against any rival power that might be credited with the dark half (Westermann, Isaiah 40-66, OTL 1969; Blenkinsopp, Isaiah 40-55, AB 19A, 2002, on the possible anti-dualist edge against Persian thought). The modern scholarly versions translate the pair non-morally (NRSV, NJPS 'weal ... woe'; ESV 'well-being ... calamity'), and the Editor follows them. ASV/KJV 'evil' is not wrong as a gloss of rāʿ, but in modern English it reads as moral wickedness, which the antithesis with šālôm does not support. The theodicy question the verse raised in later tradition is given in commentary: the Yotzer blessing of the morning liturgy (b. Ber. 11b) quotes the verse with 'creates all things' in place of 'creates evil'. 'Well-being' replaces the draft's 'peace' only at this site; šālôm stays 'peace' elsewhere in the book.

entries.lemma: maśśāʾ II 'utterance, pronouncement' (the superscription of the oracles against the nations, Isa 13-23)
entries.literal: a lifting up (of the voice); pronouncement
entries.standardEnglish: the burden of (ASV, KJV); the oracle concerning (NRSV); the 'Babylon' pronouncement (NJPS)
entries.wohChoice: 'The oracle concerning Babylon' (13:1), 'this oracle' (14:28), 'The oracle concerning Moab' (15:1); 'burden' is kept in commentary only.
entries.rationale: maśśāʾ is a homonym. maśśāʾ I is a 'load, burden' (from nśʾ 'lift, carry'), and maśśāʾ II, used in prophetic headings, is a 'pronouncement', probably from the idiom nāśāʾ qôl 'lift up the voice' (HALOT; DCH; Weis, A Definition of the Genre Maśśāʾ, 1986). The traditional 'burden' (KJV, ASV) comes from reading the first sense into the second. Jer 23:33-38 plays on the double sense, which shows the two were felt as related, but it does not make 'burden' the meaning of the heading. The modern versions (NRSV 'oracle', NJPS 'pronouncement') and the commentators (Wildberger, Isaiah 13-27, 1997; Blenkinsopp, Isaiah 1-39, AB 19, 2000) read the heading as a genre label. 'Oracle' is chosen as the established English term, and the same rendering will govern the remaining maśśāʾ headings of Isa 13-23 and 30:6.

entries.translit: kᵉṯîḇ / qᵉrê; nᵉquddôṯ (puncta extraordinaria); the Great Isaiah Scroll
entries.strongs: n/a (text-critical policy)
entries.lemma: the textual basis of the Isaiah line: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), qere read, ketiv and Qumran variants in commentary
entries.literal: what is written / what is read
entries.standardEnglish: ASV generally follows the qere; NRSV adopts 1QIsaᵃ or LXX readings at several sites; NJPS follows MT
entries.wohChoice: The line translates the Masoretic Text and, at ketiv/qere sites, the qere: 13:16, 29:11, 32:7, 32:15, 42:20, 42:24, 44:17, 44:24, 45:2, 54:16, 65:4, 65:7. At 13:16 the qere's euphemism tiššāḵaḇnāh is rendered by its sense, 'ravished' (the ketiv's sense is the same act), because 'lain with' misreports the violence. The extraordinary points over hēmmāh at 44:9 are kept in the source text and the word is translated. Variants of the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaᵃ) and the ancient versions are reported in commentary and not adopted in the line: 14:4 marhēḇāh; 14:30 ʾahărōḡ; 15:9 Dibon; 40:6 'and I said'; 43:19 'paths'; 45:2 hărārîm; 45:8 wyprḥ; 48:1 mmʿy; 48:10 bḥntykh; 48:11 ʾyḥl; 54:9 kymy; 54:13 bwnyky.
entries.rationale: The project's Hebrew source is the Leningrad Codex as encoded by the Westminster Leningrad Codex, and the Isaiah overlay has followed the qere at ketiv/qere sites since chapter 25 (`madmenah-ketiv-qere-moab-isaiah-25`, `ketiv-qere-door-indignation-isaiah-26`). That keeps the line tied to the received reading tradition and makes the text-critical apparatus auditable. Qumran variants are given in full in commentary because 1QIsaᵃ is the oldest complete witness to the book (Ulrich and Flint, DJD 32, 2010) and several of its readings are adopted by NRSV. Adopting them case by case in the line, however, would make the base text eclectic in a way the rest of the corpus is not (Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 3rd ed. 2012). Three ketiv/qere pairs change the sense. At 13:16 the qere is a euphemism for a word the scribes would not read aloud; both describe rape, and the line gives that sense, 'ravished', rather than a literal 'lain with' that hides it. At 32:7 the qere 'the poor' replaces the ketiv 'the humble'. At 44:24 the qere mēʾittî 'by myself' replaces the ketiv question mî ʾittî 'who was with me?'; both deny that anyone helped in creation. The puncta extraordinaria at 44:9 mark a word the scribes doubted (Masorah; Yeivin, Introduction to the Tiberian Masorah, §80), but the word is in the text and is translated. At 48:11 the LXX supplies 'my name' (as ASV and NRSV do); only 1QIsaᵃ attests the first-person ʾyḥl (corrected at the wave I2 sign-off). Isaiah 1 (wave I-1): MT kept at 1:7 kᵉmahpēḵaṯ zārîm (emendation sᵉḏōm in commentary), 1:12 lērāʾôṯ (Niphal pointing kept; Qal 'to see my face' in commentary), 1:13 ʾāwen (LXX 'fasting' = ṣôm in commentary), 1:29 yēḇōšû (MT person shift kept; NRSV's second-person rendering in commentary). 1:31 ûp̄ōʿălô: MT participial pointing followed, 'its maker' (ASV/NRSV noun 'his work', on a repointing, in commentary; founder ruling 2026-11-26). Wave I-1 (Isa 2): 1QIsaᵃ minus at 2:9b-10 and LXX minus of 2:22 reported in commentary, MT kept; at 2:20 the one-word reading laḥăp̄arpērôṯ 'moles' is followed against the Leningrad word division (consonants unchanged; a word-division exception, founder sign-off 2026-11-26). Wave I-1 (Isa 3): qere read at 3:15 (mah-lāḵem for the joined ketiv mlkm) and 3:16 (nᵉṭûyôṯ for nṭwwt); Masoretic readings kept, with the alternatives reported in commentary, at 3:10 (conjectural ʾašrê 'happy'; Old Greek 'let us bind the righteous'), 3:12 (Old Greek 'glean' for mᵉʿôlēl and 'creditors' for nāšîm), 3:13 (Old Greek and Syriac 'his people' for ʿammîm) and 3:24 (1QIsaᵃ adds bwšt 'shame', making kî a conjunction; MT noun kî 'branding' kept). Wave I-1: at 4:5 MT ûḇārāʾ and miqrāʾehā are kept; the LXX readings kai hēxei ('and he will come') and 'all the places around it' are reported in commentary. Wave I-3 (Isa 7): chapter 7 has no ketiv/qere pair. Kept in the line against literary-critical proposals, which are reported in commentary: 7:8b the sixty-five-year clause (often taken as a gloss and sometimes transposed after 7:9a, as NJPS prints it); 7:17 ʾēṯ meleḵ ʾaššûr and 7:20 bᵉmeleḵ ʾaššûr (often taken as explanatory glosses). Kept against a repointing: 7:11 šᵉʾālāh 'ask' (repointed šᵉʾōlāh 'to Sheol' by NRSV and NJPS and reflected in the Vulgate). Reported: 7:14 the Septuagint's second-person kaléseis 'you shall call' (verified); 1QIsaᵃ wqrʾ for MT wᵉqārāʾṯ (not verified). Orchestrator: add these sites to the variant list in wohChoice on merge; the Editor does not rewrite the field here, to avoid a conflict with the parallel Editors. Wave I-3 (Isa 8): MT kept and variants reported, not adopted: 8:2 imperative 'and take witnesses' of 1QIsaᵃ and the versions (not verified; NJPS renders in that sense) for the MT cohortative wᵉʾāʿîḏāh; 8:6 conjectural ûmāsôs 'and melting' for ûmᵉśôś; 8:11 1QIsaᵃ swr 'turned me aside' for wᵉyissᵉrēnî (not verified); 8:12 conjectural qōdeš 'holy' for qešer; 8:14 conjectural môqēš / forms of qdš for miqdāš; 8:23 1QIsaᵃ reading behind NJPS 'if there were to be' for lōʾ (attested by the NJPS footnote, verified on Sefaria). No ketiv/qere site in chapter 8. Wave I-3 (Isa 9): two ketiv/qere sites follow the qere. At 9:2 the qere lô 'to it' replaces the ketiv lōʾ 'not', giving 'you have increased its joy' (ASV) against KJV's ketiv reading; the conjectural redivision haggîlāh 'the exultation' alters the consonants and is reported only. At 9:6 the ketiv writes a final mem inside lᵉmarbēh (לםרבה), and the qere is the normal form; this changes the spelling only, and the emendation lāhem rabbāh and the Talmud's reading of the closed mem (b. Sanh. 94a) are given in commentary. Wave I-3 (Isa 10): the qere is translated at 10:6 (ûlᵉśûmô), 10:13 (waʿăṯûḏôṯêhem 'their treasures') and 10:32 (baṯ 'the daughter of Zion'). MT is kept, with the alternatives reported in commentary, at five sites: 10:4 (Lagarde's Beltis/Osiris redivision); 10:5 (hûʾ bᵉyāḏām, deleted by many as a gloss); 10:12 (MT ʾep̄qōḏ 'I will punish'; LXX, Syriac and NRSV third person); 10:25 (taḇlîṯām; emendation ʿal-tēḇēl yittōm); 10:27 (mippᵉnê-šāmen and the MT verse division; NRSV emendation 'He has gone up from Rimmon'). The MT pointing is also kept at 10:30 (ʿăniyyāh 'poor'; repointed ʿănîhā 'answer her', NRSV). Wave I-3 (Isa 11): MT kept and alternatives reported in commentary at 11:1 yip̄reh 'shall bear fruit' (LXX, Vulgate 'come up / sprout'); 11:4 the second ʾereṣ (emendation ʿārîṣ 'the ruthless', NJPS note); 11:6 the verbless ûmᵉrîʾ yaḥdāw (1QIsaᵃ and LXX 'shall feed', NJPS note); 11:11 yāḏô without a governing verb (proposed lišʾēṯ, not verified); 11:15 wᵉheḥĕrîm 'devote to destruction' (heḥĕrîḇ 'dry up', NJPS, probably LXX). Wave I-3 (Isa 12): at 12:5 the qere mûḏaʿaṯ (Hophal participle) is translated. The ketiv מידעת has the consonants of the Pual participle, and the sense 'made known' is the same. Orchestrator: add '12:5' to the qere list in wohChoice on merge. This is a scope-only change, and the Editor does not rewrite the field here, to avoid a conflict with the parallel Editors.

entries.strongs: H5612 (sēp̄er); H2856 (ḥāṯam); H3045 (yāḏaʿ)
entries.lemma: sēp̄er 'written document, scroll, letter'; yôḏēaʿ sēp̄er 'one who knows writing' (= literate)
entries.partOfSpeech: noun + passive participle; participle + noun idiom
entries.literal: the sealed writing; one knowing writing
entries.standardEnglish: a book that is sealed; one that is learned (ASV); a sealed document; those who can read (NRSV)
entries.wohChoice: 'a sealed scroll' (29:11), 'the scroll' (29:12), 'the words of a scroll' (29:18); the idiom yôḏēaʿ sēp̄er kept literally, 'one who knows writing' / 'I do not know writing'.
entries.rationale: In the eighth century sēp̄er is any written document (letter, deed, scroll), and a 'sealed' sēp̄er is a rolled document closed with a seal impression, like the deed of purchase in Jer 32:10-14 (BDB; HALOT; Wildberger, Isaiah 28-39, 2002). English 'book' (ASV) suggests a bound codex and, in this verse, a particular book. 'Scroll' gives the physical object accurately (NIV 'scroll'; NRSV and NJPS 'document') without suggesting which writing is meant. That matters here because the reception text applies 29:12 to the Bible (see the reception note at 29:12), and the line should not make that application easier than the Hebrew does. The idiom yôḏēaʿ sēp̄er ('knowing writing', i.e. literate) is kept literally rather than as ASV's 'learned', so the reader can see that the same noun names the sealed document and the skill of reading it. The ketiv has-sēp̄er (with article) / qere sēp̄er at 29:11 is governed by `mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`.

entries.strongs: H740 (ʾărîʾēl)
entries.lemma: ʾărîʾēl, the cipher-name for Jerusalem
entries.partOfSpeech: proper noun (with wordplay on the common noun ʾărîʾēl "altar-hearth")
entries.literal: Ariel (altar-hearth / lion of El)
entries.standardEnglish: Ariel (ASV, NRSV, NJPS)
entries.wohChoice: 'Ariel' transliterated at 29:1, 2, 7 (with 'like an Ariel' at v2, the altar-hearth wordplay explained in commentary). ʾôḇ 'a ghost' at 29:4 is governed by ob-yiddeoni-ghosts-familiar-spirits-isaiah (founder ruling 2026-11-26).
entries.rationale: ʾărîʾēl is a cipher for Jerusalem ('the city where David encamped'). Ezek 43:15-16 uses the same word for the altar-hearth, and Isa 29:2 plays on that sense: Jerusalem 'shall be to me like an ʾărîʾēl', a place of burning. Because the name and the wordplay depend on keeping one word, the line transliterates with ASV, NRSV and NJPS, and the commentary explains the pun and the alternative derivation 'lion of El' (Wildberger, Isaiah 28-39; Blenkinsopp, AB 19). The ʾôḇ simile of 29:4 ('like that of a ghost from the ground'), formerly governed here, was moved in wave I-3 to ob-yiddeoni-ghosts-familiar-spirits-isaiah (founder ruling 2026-11-26), so that ʾôḇ 'ghost' is governed by one entry at 8:19 and 29:4; the reasons for 'a ghost' against ASV's 'one that hath a familiar spirit' are recorded there. The id is kept unchanged for the stability of existing references.

entries.translit: ḥasdô; ham-mᵉsukkān; ḥērem; pûḵ; māšāl; hab-bayiṯ; śᵉʿîrîm; kᵉsîlêhem; bᵉrîḥehā
entries.strongs: H2617 (ḥeseḏ); H5533 (mᵉsukkān, Akkadian musukkannu); H2764 (ḥērem); H6320 (pûḵ); H4912 (māšāl); H1004 (bayiṯ); H8163 (śāʿîr); H3685 (kᵉsîl); H1281 (bārîaḥ 'fugitive')
entries.lemma: single-site lexical decisions of the Isaiah wave I2
entries.literal: its loyalty; the musukkannu-wood; the ban; antimony; saying/taunt; the house; hairy ones; their Orions; her fugitives
entries.standardEnglish: goodliness; he that is impoverished; the curse; fair colors; parable; Bayith; wild goats; constellations (ASV); her nobles (ASV 15:5)
entries.wohChoice: 40:6 ḥasdô 'its constancy' (NRSV); 40:20 ham-mᵉsukkān 'sissoo wood' (tᵉrûmāh 'oblation' under the central qorbanot entry) (Akkadian musukkannu; NRSV 'mulberry wood'); 43:28 laḥ-ḥērem 'to be devoted to destruction' (central cherem-devote-to-destruction-cross-corpus); 54:11 bap-pûḵ 'in antimony' (NRSV); 14:4 māšāl 'taunt' (NRSV); 15:2 hab-bayiṯ 'the temple' (NJPS); 13:21 śᵉʿîrîm 'wild goats' (ASV kept; 'goat-demons' in commentary); 13:10 kᵉsîlêhem 'their constellations' (ASV kept). 15:5 bᵉrîḥehā 'her fugitives' (KJV, NRSV, NJPS; ASV 'her nobles' recorded in commentary).
entries.rationale: Each item is a site where the draft's ASV wording rests on a lexical identification that modern lexicography has revised, or where ASV's English has shifted in meaning. The Editor adopts the revised sense in the line only where the Masoretic consonants support it without emendation. (1) ḥeseḏ applied to 'all flesh' at 40:6 is human constancy or loyalty, which is as brief as the flower of the field. ASV's 'goodliness' (beauty) follows LXX doxa, not the Hebrew; NRSV 'constancy', and Westermann and Blenkinsopp read 'loyalty'. The central `chesed-solitary-covenant-kindness` entry is not applied to this human, non-covenantal use. (2) mᵉsukkān at 40:20 is the Akkadian loanword musukkannu, a durable hardwood, probably Dalbergia sissoo (CAD M/2 237-240; HALOT; NRSV, NJPS). ASV's 'he that is impoverished' derives the form from skn 'be poor', a derivation abandoned since the Akkadian word was identified. (3) ḥērem at 43:28 is the sacral ban, total destruction devoted to the deity (Lohfink, TDOT 5:180-199). ASV's 'curse' blurs it with ʾālāh / qᵉlālāh. (4) pûḵ at 54:11 is antimony or kohl, the dark eye-paint of 2 Kgs 9:30, used here for the dark setting of the gemstones (NRSV); ASV's 'fair colors' is a guess. (5) māšāl at 14:4 is a mocking song in context (NRSV 'taunt', NJPS 'song of scorn'); English 'parable' now means a moral story and misleads. (6) hab-bayiṯ at 15:2 has the article and is most naturally 'the temple' of Kemosh (NJPS), not a place name 'Bayith' (ASV). (7) At 13:21 and 13:10 the ASV renderings are kept ('wild goats'; 'their constellations'), and the alternatives ('goat-demons', cf. Lev 17:7; 'their Orions') are given in commentary, because the mythological sense of śᵉʿîrîm is possible but not required by the ruin-fauna list. (8) Added at the wave I2 sign-off (2026-11-01, Reviewer revise ratified): bᵉrîḥehā at 15:5 is 'her fugitives' (from bārîaḥ 'fugitive'; BDB, HALOT, KJV, NRSV, NJPS, Wildberger, Blenkinsopp). The Masoretic vowels are irregular for both 'her bar' and a plural 'her fugitives', so the pointing does not decide; ASV's 'her nobles' (bars = defenders) is the more interpretive reading, and with it the supplied verb 'flee' has no basis in the noun.

entries.lemma: hôy (interjection of lament and threat)
entries.literal: ah! / alas! / woe!
entries.standardEnglish: Ah (ASV, NRSV, NJPS at 1:4, 1:24); Woe (ASV/NRSV in most 'woe-oracle' openings, e.g. 5:8; 29:1; 45:9)
entries.wohChoice: 'Woe' for hôy throughout Isaiah: vocative 'Woe, sinful nation' (1:4), as 'Woe, Ariel' (29:1); 'Woe to …' before a participle or preposition (29:15; 45:9, 10; the woe-series of 5:8-22); absolute 'Woe!' introducing a divine threat (1:24).
entries.rationale: hôy is the cry of the funeral lament (1 Kgs 13:30; Jer 22:18; 34:5), which the eighth-century prophets turned into the opening of the woe-oracle against the living (Westermann, Basic Forms of Prophetic Speech, 1967; Gerstenberger, 'The Woe-Oracles of the Prophets', JBL 81, 1962; Wildberger, Isaiah 1-12, on 5:8). The English versions render it by context, 'Ah' where it stands alone and 'Woe' where it is followed by 'to' or a participle, so the same Hebrew word appears under two English words in one book. The signed-off Isaiah chapters already print 'Woe' at 29:1, 15 and 45:9, 10, and the wave I-1 ruling extends that rendering to every hôy in Isaiah so that readers can trace the form. At 1:24 the cry introduces YHWH's threat against his adversaries; NJPS 'Ah' is the more idiomatic English there, and the uniform 'Woe!' is accepted for consistency and noted in commentary. The claim is direct: 'woe' is a standard lexical equivalent of hôy (BDB, HALOT), and no interpretive reading is added. Recommend adding the signed-off sites ISA-29:1, 29:15, 45:9, 45:10 to appliesTo at merge (their paragraph glossaryRefs were not edited in this wave). Wave I-3 (Isa 10): 'Woe to …' before the participle at 10:1 (the woe-oracle 10:1-4, often counted with the series of 5:8-22) and the vocative 'Woe, Assyria' at 10:5 (as 'Woe, Ariel', 29:1).

entries.lemma: ʾāḏôn 'lord, master', singular with the definite article, used absolutely as a divine title before YHWH ṣᵉḇāʾôṯ (not ʾăḏōnāy H136)
entries.partOfSpeech: noun (masculine singular, definite), divine title in apposition
entries.literal: the lord / the master
entries.standardEnglish: the Sovereign (NRSV; NJPS, checked against Sefaria at 10:16, 33); the Lord (ASV, KJV, which give ʾāḏôn and ʾăḏōnāy the same English)
entries.wohChoice: 'the Sovereign' for hā-ʾāḏôn, the articular title before 'YHWH of hosts', at every Isaiah site: 1:24 'the Sovereign, YHWH of hosts, the Mighty One of Israel'; 3:1 'the Sovereign, YHWH of hosts'; and the later sites 10:16, 10:33 and 19:4. The title ʾăḏōnāy (adonai-standalone-title-isaiah) and the compound ʾăḏōnāy YHWH (adonai-yhwh-compound-isaiah-25) stay 'the Lord'. Commentary names the Hebrew hā-ʾāḏôn at each site. Founder ruling 2026-11-26 (wave I-1 decision 1, option B).
entries.rationale: Isaiah uses two different words that English traditionally renders 'the Lord': the title ʾăḏōnāy, a plural of majesty with a fossilised suffix (6:1, 8, 11; 29:13; 3:17, 18; overlay adonai-standalone-title-isaiah), and the common noun ʾāḏôn 'lord, master' with the article, hā-ʾāḏôn, which occurs in the book only in a fixed formula before YHWH ṣᵉḇāʾôṯ (1:24; 3:1; 10:16, 33; 19:4; cf. Exod 23:17; 34:23 hā-ʾāḏōn YHWH). Neither the ʾăḏōnāy entry nor the compound entry adonai-yhwh-compound-isaiah-25 covers the articular form. hā-ʾāḏôn is a royal or proprietary title, the master who owns and commands (HALOT s.v. ʾāḏôn; Jenni, TLOT 1:23-29; Eissfeldt, TDOT 1:59-72). Three standard renderings were weighed: ASV and KJV 'the Lord', which is accurate but gives ʾāḏôn and ʾăḏōnāy the same English; 'the Master', the literal sense, which is less idiomatic as a divine title; and 'the Sovereign', used by NRSV and NJPS (NJPS checked at 10:16, 33). The founder ruling of 2026-11-26 adopts 'the Sovereign', because the book's divine-name house style keeps distinct Hebrew titles distinct in English, and this rendering makes the difference visible in the line, not only in the commentary. The claim is direct: every option is a standard rendering of the noun and no lens is involved. This entry absorbs ha-adon-definite-title-isaiah, proposed for 3:1 by the chapter 3 Editor (merged at the wave I-1 merge, appliesTo united). The sites 10:16 and 10:33 are added by the wave I-3 diffs; 19:4 takes the same rendering when that chapter is translated. Wave I-3 (Isa 10): hā-ʾāḏôn YHWH ṣᵉḇāʾôṯ at 10:16 and 10:33 is rendered 'the Sovereign, YHWH of hosts' (wave I-1 decision 1, option B; founder ruling 2026-11-26), as NJPS renders the phrase at 10:16 ('The Sovereign LORD of Hosts'). Only this id is carried at these sites; ha-adon-definite-title-isaiah is merged into it.

entries.strongs: H424 (ʾēlāh); H352 (ʾayil III, pl. ʾêlîm 'great trees, terebinths'); H437 (ʾallôn)
entries.lemma: tree names: ʾēlāh / ʾayil 'terebinth' (Pistacia) and ʾallôn 'oak' (Quercus)
entries.literal: terebinth; great trees; oak
entries.standardEnglish: oak / oaks (ASV, NRSV at 1:29-30); terebinth(s) (NJPS)
entries.wohChoice: 'terebinth' for ʾēlāh and 'terebinths' for ʾêlîm (1:29, 30; 6:13 'like the terebinth'); 'oak' for ʾallôn (6:13 'and like the oak'; 44:14; 2:13 'the oaks of Bashan').
entries.rationale: Hebrew distinguishes ʾēlāh (with the related ʾayil, plural ʾêlîm), the terebinth Pistacia atlantica / palaestina, from ʾallôn, the oak (HALOT; Zohary, Plants of the Bible, 1982; Hepper, Illustrated Encyclopedia of Bible Plants, 1992). The ASV and NRSV render both 'oak' at 1:29-30, which erases the distinction that 6:13 depends on ('like the terebinth and like the oak'), where the signed-off overlay already prints the two names separately (levaer-massevet-stump-isaiah). NJPS renders 'terebinths / terebinth' at 1:29-30. Using one English word per Hebrew tree name keeps the book consistent and lets readers see that the trees of the cultic sites in 1:29 are the same species as the felled tree of 6:13. The claim is direct because the botanical identification is lexical consensus and the change adds no interpretation.

entries.translit: pāšʿû bî; pōšʿîm; ʿal meh; baṯ-ṣiyyôn; nᵉṣûrāh; śārîḏ kimʿāṭ; qᵉṭōreṯ; môʿăḏêḵem; ʾaššᵉrû ḥāmôṣ; wᵉniwwāḵᵉḥāh; ʾennāḥēm; kabbōr; bᵉḏîlāyiḵ; wᵉšāḇêhā; he-ḥāsōn; nᵉʿōreṯ; ûp̄ōʿălô
entries.strongs: H6586 (pāšaʿ); H5921 + H4100 (ʿal meh); H1323 + H6726 (baṯ ṣiyyôn); H5341 (nāṣar); H8300 (śārîḏ); H4592 (mᵉʿaṭ); H7004 (qᵉṭōreṯ); H4150 (môʿēḏ); H833 (ʾāšar Piel); H2541 (ḥāmôṣ); H3198 (yākaḥ); H5162 (nāḥam); H1252 / H1253 (bōr 'cleanness' / 'lye'); H913 (bᵉḏîl); H7725 (šûḇ); H2634 (ḥāsōn); H5296 (nᵉʿōreṯ); H6466 (pāʿal, Qal participle pōʿēl, as pointed) / H6467 (pōʿal, the repointed noun)
entries.lemma: single-site lexical and syntactic decisions of Isaiah 1
entries.literal: they rebelled against me; on what?; daughter of Zion; watched; a survivor, a little; incense / smoke; your appointed times; set right the oppressed/ruthless; let us dispute; I will relieve myself; as (with) cleanness / lye; your tin; her returning ones; the strong; tow; its maker (participle, as pointed) / his work (noun, repointed)
entries.standardEnglish: ASV throughout, with NRSV/NJPS alternatives as listed in wohChoice
entries.wohChoice: 1:2 pāšʿû bî 'they have rebelled against me' (ASV, NRSV, NJPS; 43:27 'transgressed' is kept there); 1:28 pōšʿîm 'transgressors' (ASV), keeping pšʿ distinct from sôrᵉrîm 'rebels' (1:23); 1:5 ʿal meh 'Why' (ASV; locative 'on what part?' in commentary); 1:8 baṯ-ṣiyyôn 'the daughter of Zion' (corpus wording; appositional sense in commentary) and nᵉṣûrāh 'besieged' (nṣr in the blockade sense, Jer 4:16); 1:9 śārîḏ kimʿāṭ 'a very small remnant' following the accents (central she-erit NOT applied: śārîḏ is not šᵉʾērîṯ); 1:13 qᵉṭōreṯ 'incense' (ASV); 1:14 môʿăḏêḵem 'your appointed feasts' (ASV; central moadim NOT extended); 1:17 ʾaššᵉrû ḥāmôṣ 'relieve the oppressed' (LXX, Vulgate, ASV, NRSV, NJPS; active 'correct the oppressor' in commentary); 1:18 wᵉniwwāḵᵉḥāh 'let us reason together' (ASV; forensic sense in commentary) with the conditionals as promises; 1:24 ʾennāḥēm miṣṣāray 'I will ease myself of my adversaries' (ASV); 1:25 kabbōr 'thoroughly' (ASV; 'as with lye' in commentary) and bᵉḏîlāyiḵ 'your tin' (ASV; 'alloy' in commentary); 1:27 wᵉšāḇêhā 'those of her who return' (ambiguity of šûḇ kept); 1:31 he-ḥāsōn 'the strong', nᵉʿōreṯ 'tinder' (NRSV, NJPS; ASV 'tow'), ûp̄ōʿălô 'its maker', following the MT pointing of the suffixed Qal participle pōʿēl (Job 36:3 lᵉp̄ōʿălî 'to my Maker'); 'his work' (ASV, NRSV, on the repointing pāʿŏlô) in commentary (founder ruling 2026-11-26).
entries.rationale: Each item is a site where the Translator's draft follows the ASV and the modern versions or lexica offer a defensible alternative. The Editor keeps the standard rendering in the line where it is supported by the Masoretic consonants and accents, by the ancient versions, or by the lexica, and reports the alternative in commentary, so that the text stays a conventional scholarly rendering and the apparatus shows the choice. (1) pšʿ: the verb with bᵉ- of a person is breach of a relationship (Knierim, TLOT 2:1033-1037); 'rebelled' suits the parent-child frame of 1:2, while 'transgressors' at 1:28 avoids collapsing pšʿ, srr (1:23) and mrh (1:20) into one English word. (2) 1:9 follows the athnach, as ASV does; śārîḏ is a survivor (BDB, HALOT), not the remnant-keyword governed by the central she-erit entry. (3) 1:17: both ancient versions read ḥāmôṣ as passive (LXX rhysasthe adikoumenon; Vulgate subvenite oppresso), while BDB's 'ruthless' supports the active reading of RSV; the versions decide. (4) 1:18: ykḥ Niphal is forensic (HALOT 'argue a case'); 'reason together' is kept as the established English and the court setting is stated in the note. (5) 1:25: bōr is either 'cleanness' (ASV 'thoroughly') or 'lye' (HALOT, NRSV, NJPS); both are lexically attested, and the ASV is kept under the rule that a correct draft is preserved. (6) 1:31: the Masoretic vowels of ûp̄ōʿălô (holem, hatef patah) are those of the suffixed Qal participle, as at Job 36:3, whereas the noun pōʿal with suffix is pointed pāʿŏlô (Jer 22:13; Prov 20:11). Under the book's rule that the line translates the pointed MT (applied at 1:12), the line reads 'and its maker a spark', and the noun reading 'his work' of ASV and NRSV, which presupposes a repointing, is reported in commentary (founder ruling 2026-11-26, wave I-1 decision 3). No item carries a project-specific reading, so the claim type is direct.

entries.strongs: H120 (ʾāḏām); H376 (ʾîš, with ʾănāšîm as its plural)
entries.lemma: ʾāḏām as the generic collective noun in Isaiah, alone and in the ʾāḏām / ʾîš refrain
entries.literal: human(s), humankind / man, each one, anyone / men, people
entries.standardEnglish: ASV 'the mean man … the great man' (2:9; 5:15), 'man' / 'men' elsewhere; NRSV 'people … everyone' (2:9; 5:15), 'everyone' (2:11), 'mortals … their … they' (2:22); NJPS 'man … mortal'
entries.wohChoice: 'humankind' for ʾāḏām / hā-ʾāḏām used generically (2:9, 11, 17, 20, 22; 5:15; as already printed at 29:19 and 45:12); 'everyone' for ʾîš in the synonymous refrain wayyiššaḥ ʾāḏām wayyišpal-ʾîš ('So humankind is bowed down, and everyone is brought low', 2:9; 'And humankind is bowed down, and everyone is brought low', 5:15); 'human' for ʾănāšîm in the parallel colon rûm ʾănāšîm, 'human loftiness' (2:11, 17). Pronoun rule: the collective hā-ʾāḏām takes English plural pronouns, although the Hebrew suffixes and pronouns are singular (2:20 'their idols of silver … which they made for themselves'; 2:22 'who have breath in their nostrils; for of what account are they?'). ʾîš and ʾănāšîm outside the refrain (e.g. 'men of Judah', 5:3, 7) are not governed by this entry. Founder ruling 2026-11-26 (wave I-1 decision 2, option C1).
entries.rationale: In Isa 2 and 5 ʾāḏām is the generic collective for human beings set against YHWH, who 'alone shall be exalted' (2:11, 17), and the book's stable chapters already render it 'humankind' (29:19 'the poorest of humankind'; 45:12 'I created humankind upon it'), the NRSV-type inclusive rendering of the collective. The refrain wayyiššaḥ ʾāḏām wayyišpal-ʾîš (2:9; 5:15) was read by ASV and KJV as a social contrast ('the mean man … the great man'), on the model of bᵉnê ʾāḏām … bᵉnê ʾîš in Ps 49:3 and 62:10; without bᵉnê the nouns are most naturally a synonymous pair, as NRSV, NJPS, Wildberger (Isaiah 1-12, 1991) and Williamson (Isaiah 1-5, ICC, 2006) take them, and BDB records ʾîš in the generic sense 'each, anyone' in parallel with ʾāḏām. The draft rendered the pair 'humankind … man', which set a neutral and a gender-marked English word side by side for two synonyms. The founder ruling of 2026-11-26 (option C1, recommended by the Reviewer) gives ʾîš its generic sense, 'everyone', as NRSV does ('people … everyone'), so the line reads 'humankind is bowed down, and everyone is brought low' at both 2:9 and 5:15. In the parallel colon of 2:11 and 2:17, rûm ʾănāšîm ('the loftiness of men'; ʾănāšîm serves as the plural of ʾîš) is rendered 'human loftiness'. The alternative 'the loftiness of all people' was considered and not adopted, because the Hebrew has no kol 'all'; the adjective keeps the parallel with 'humankind' and adds no word. The pronoun rule follows from the same ruling: the collective hā-ʾāḏām takes English plural pronouns. At 2:20 the plural verb ʿāśû already governs the relative clause, so the singular suffixes of kaspô, zᵉhāḇô and lô are rendered 'their … themselves' (NRSV, ASV); at 2:22 the singular bᵉʾappô and hûʾ are rendered 'their nostrils … are they' (NRSV 'who have only breath in their nostrils … of what account are they?'). Both rules are standard English practice for a Hebrew collective and change no sense. The central entries are not applied: ha-adam ('the human') is scoped to Genesis 2-3, where the article marks the first human, and adam-adamah is applied in Isaiah only at ʾădāmāh 'ground' sites. The entry is direct because every rendering is attested in the standard versions and no reading is added. ISA-5:15 is governed here; the chapter 5 Editor proposed no separate entry.

entries.strongs: H1926 (hāḏār); H1347 (gāʾôn)
entries.lemma: hāḏār 'splendour, adornment' in construct with gāʾôn 'majesty, eminence'
entries.literal: the splendour of his eminence
entries.standardEnglish: the glory of his majesty (ASV, NRSV); his dread majesty (NJPS)
entries.wohChoice: 'the splendor of his majesty' (2:10, 19, 21): hāḏār 'splendor' (as at 53:2 'no splendor'), gāʾôn 'majesty' (as at 24:14 'the majesty of YHWH'); 'glory' is reserved for kāḇôḏ.
entries.rationale: hāḏār is 'ornament, splendour, honour' (BDB; HALOT; Warmuth, TDOT 3:335-341), and gāʾôn is 'height, eminence, majesty' (BDB; HALOT); ASV's 'the glory of his majesty' is a fair English rendering in isolation. In this corpus, however, 'glory' is the fixed English for kāḇôḏ (central kavod-yhwh, applied at Isa 40:5), and Isaiah sets the two nouns side by side in a single verse ('the glory of Lebanon … the splendour of Carmel … the glory of YHWH, the splendour of our God', 35:2), so a shared English word would hide a distinction the Hebrew draws. The stable chapters already render hāḏār 'splendor' (53:2) and gāʾôn 'majesty' (24:14), and the change keeps the book concordant. 'Splendor' is a standard lexical gloss of hāḏār and carries no interpretive load, so the claim is direct.

entries.strongs: H7914 (śᵉḵiyyāh); H2532 (ḥemdāh)
entries.lemma: śᵉḵiyyāh, a hapax of disputed sense; with ḥemdāh 'desire, delight'
entries.partOfSpeech: noun (feminine plural, construct) + noun with article
entries.literal: the ?ships / ?images of delight
entries.standardEnglish: pleasant imagery (ASV); pleasant pictures (KJV); the beautiful craft (NRSV); the gallant barks (NJPS)
entries.wohChoice: 'all the beautiful vessels' (2:16), in parallel with 'all the ships of Tarshish'.
entries.rationale: The noun occurs only here. ASV and KJV derive it from śkh 'look' (compare maśkîṯ 'carved figure', Lev 26:1; Num 33:52) and render 'pleasant imagery / pictures'. Modern lexicography connects it with an Egyptian word for a ship and reads the line as synonymous parallelism with ʾŏniyyôṯ taršîš 'ships of Tarshish' (HALOT s.v.; Wildberger, Isaiah 1-12, 1991; Blenkinsopp, Isaiah 1-39, AB 19, 2000); NRSV ('the beautiful craft') and NJPS ('the gallant barks') follow, and the LXX 'every sight of beautiful ships' already combines both senses. As with the Akkadian loanword at 40:20 (lexical-cruxes-wave-i2-isaiah), the revised identification is adopted because the Masoretic consonants support it without emendation. 'Vessels' is chosen over NRSV 'craft' to keep a separate English word from 'ships' and to stay unambiguously nautical, since 'craft' in present-day English also denotes aircraft; the lens-salient reading of this site is confined to a labelled apparatus note. The claim is inferred rather than direct because the loanword etymology is a well-supported proposal, not a certainty, and the traditional English versions read otherwise.

entries.translit: bᵉrōʾš; nāhărû; hôḵîaḥ lᵉ-; ʾittîm; mālᵉʾû miqqedem; yaśpîqû; nāṭaštāh; wᵉšāp̄ēl; laʿărōṣ; laḥpōr pērôṯ
entries.strongs: H7218 (rōʾš); H5102 (nāhar); H3198 (ykḥ); H855 (ʾēṯ); H6924 (qedem); H5606 (spq); H5203 (nṭš); H8213 (šāp̄ēl); H6206 (ʿāraṣ); H2661 + H6512 (Strong's follows the two-word division at 2:20)
entries.lemma: single-site lexical and textual decisions of Isaiah 2
entries.literal: at the head of; they shall stream; arbitrate for; ploughing tools; they are full from the east; they clap / abound; you have forsaken; and low; to terrify; to dig holes / to moles
entries.standardEnglish: ASV throughout; NRSV 'as the highest of', 'stream', 'arbitrate', 'to terrify'; NJPS 'gaze with joy', 'abound', 'overawe', 'flying foxes'
entries.wohChoice: 2:2 'on the top of the mountains … shall flow to it' (ASV); 2:4 'shall decide for many peoples … plowshares' (ASV/NJPS); 2:6 'they are full from the east' with no supplement, 'they strike hands with' (spq I), MT 2ms 'you have forsaken' kept; 2:12 MT wᵉšāp̄ēl 'and it shall be brought low' kept (emendation gāḇōah in commentary); 2:19, 21 laʿărōṣ 'to terrify' (NRSV; ASV 'shake mightily'); 2:20 one-word reading laḥăp̄arpērôṯ 'to the moles' (ASV, NRSV, NJPS) against the Leningrad two-word division (founder sign-off 2026-11-26).
entries.rationale: Each item is a site where the Translator flagged a choice between standard renderings; the Editor keeps the Masoretic text and the ASV wording unless the lexicon or the Masoretic consonants support a change. (1) bᵉrōʾš hehārîm is spatial 'on the top of' (BDB rōʾš), and nhr I 'flow, stream' is preferred to NJPS nhr II 'be radiant' because the parallel Mic 4:1 and the uphill-stream image are read so by most commentators (Wildberger; Blenkinsopp). (2) The Hiphil of ykḥ with lᵉ- is to decide or arbitrate for parties (BDB; HALOT); ʾittîm is a digging or ploughing implement whose exact form is unknown (ploughshare, mattock or hoe have all been proposed), and 'plowshares' is kept as the English of all three standard versions. (3) At 2:6 the elliptical mālᵉʾû miqqedem is translated without ASV's supplement or the conjectural qōsᵉmîm; spq I 'clap, strike hands' (Job 27:23) is kept with ASV; the MT second person nāṭaštāh is kept against the LXX third person. (4) At 2:12 MT wᵉšāp̄ēl is kept; the emendation wᵉḡāḇōah (BHS; Wildberger) is reported in commentary. (5) ʿāraṣ means 'terrify, inspire awe' (BDB; HALOT), the sense it has at Isa 8:12-13, 29:23 and 47:12; ASV's 'shake mightily' is not supported by that usage, and NRSV 'terrify' and NJPS 'overawe' are followed. (6) At 2:20 the Leningrad Codex divides laḥpōr pērôṯ 'to dig holes', with no ketiv/qere note in the WLC encoding; BDB and the BHS apparatus record the one-word reading of many manuscripts and the versions, and ASV, NRSV and NJPS translate it. The consonants are unchanged, but because the word division departs from the base text the item is also recorded under mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah as a word-division exception (founder sign-off 2026-11-26).

entries.lemma: laḥaš 'whisper; whispered charm, incantation; amulet'
entries.literal: a whisper
entries.standardEnglish: enchantment, charm (3:3); amulets (3:20); prayer (26:16)
entries.wohChoice: Context-sensitive, one lemma: (a) nᵉḇôn laḥaš 'the skilled enchanter' (ISA-3:3), laḥaš as a whispered spell; (b) plural lᵉḥāšîm 'the amulets' (ISA-3:20), objects carrying a charm; (c) the hushed-prayer sense at 26:16 remains governed by its phrase entry tzaqun-lachash-whispered-prayer-isaiah-26 and is not changed.
entries.rationale: laḥaš is a whisper, and the Hebrew Bible uses it chiefly for the whispered spell of the snake-charmer or enchanter (Jer 8:17; Eccl 10:11; cf. the participle mᵉlaḥăšîm 'charmers', Ps 58:6) and once for a hushed prayer (Isa 26:16). At 3:3 nᵉḇôn laḥaš, 'one discerning in charms', closes a list of the state's leaders that also contains the qōsēm 'diviner' (3:2), so the enchanter sense is the natural one and 'the skilled enchanter' is the established rendering. At 3:20 the plural stands in a catalogue of jewellery and must be an object; the standard lexical identification is amulets, charms worn on the body, and the line says 'the amulets' (the 'earrings' of older English rests on a guessed connection between whispering and the ear and is not followed). One entry governs both Isaiah 3 sites so that the shared lemma is visible, while the 26:16 phrase ruling, a different context, is left as signed off. The renderings are standard and carry no lens, so the entry is direct (BDB, HALOT s.v.; Wildberger, Isaiah 1-12).

entries.source: מְשַׂקְּרוֹת · טָפֹף · תְּעַכַּסְנָה · שִׂפַּח · פֹּת · עֲכָסִים · שְׁבִיסִים · שַׂהֲרֹנִים · נְטִיפוֹת · שֵׁירוֹת · רְעָלוֹת · פְּאֵרִים · צְעָדוֹת · קִשֻּׁרִים · בָּתֵּי הַנֶּפֶשׁ · לְחָשִׁים · טַבָּעוֹת · נִזְמֵי הָאָף · מַחֲלָצוֹת · מַעֲטָפוֹת · מִטְפָּחוֹת · חֲרִיטִים · גִּלְיֹנִים · סְדִינִים · צְנִיפוֹת · רְדִידִים · חֲגוֹרָה · נִקְפָּה · מַעֲשֶׂה מִקְשֶׁה · פְּתִיגִיל · כִּי
entries.translit: mᵉśaqqᵉrôṯ; ṭāp̄ōp̄; tᵉʿakkasnāh; śippaḥ; pōṯ; ʿăḵāsîm; šᵉḇîsîm; śahărōnîm; nᵉṭîp̄ôṯ; šêrôṯ; rᵉʿālôṯ; pᵉʾērîm; ṣᵉʿāḏôṯ; qiššurîm; bāttê han-nep̄eš; lᵉḥāšîm; ṭabbāʿôṯ; nizmê hā-ʾap̄; maḥălāṣôṯ; maʿăṭāp̄ôṯ; miṭpāḥôṯ; ḥărîṭîm; gilyōnîm; sᵉḏînîm; ṣᵉnîp̄ôṯ; rᵉḏîḏîm; ḥăḡôrāh; nip̄qāh; maʿăśeh miqšeh; pᵉṯîḡîl; kî
entries.lemma: the daughters-of-Zion oracle (Isa 3:16-24): conduct verbs, the punishment verbs and the catalogue of finery, many items hapax legomena
entries.literal: see wohChoice; literal senses recorded in commentary
entries.standardEnglish: older English versions: cauls, mufflers, tablets/perfume-boxes, earrings, crisping pins, stomacher; modern versions vary item by item (headbands, scarves, armlets, garments of gauze)
entries.wohChoice: One conventional rendering per item and a different English word for each Hebrew word. 3:16 mᵉśaqqᵉrôṯ ʿênāyim 'wanton eyes'; ṭāp̄ōp̄ 'mincing'; tᵉʿakkasnāh 'jingling (with their feet)'. 3:17 śippaḥ 'strike with scabs'; pōṯ 'secret parts'. 3:18 ʿăḵāsîm 'anklets'; šᵉḇîsîm 'headbands' (draft 'cauls' changed); śahărōnîm 'crescents'. 3:19 nᵉṭîp̄ôṯ 'pendants'; šêrôṯ 'bracelets'; rᵉʿālôṯ 'scarves' (draft 'mufflers' changed). 3:20 pᵉʾērîm 'headdresses'; ṣᵉʿāḏôṯ 'ankle chains'; qiššurîm 'sashes'; bāttê han-nep̄eš 'perfume boxes'; lᵉḥāšîm 'amulets' (lachash-charm-amulet-isaiah). 3:21 ṭabbāʿôṯ 'rings'; nizmê hā-ʾap̄ 'nose rings'. 3:22 maḥălāṣôṯ 'festal robes'; maʿăṭāp̄ôṯ 'mantles'; miṭpāḥôṯ 'shawls'; ḥărîṭîm 'purses'. 3:23 gilyōnîm 'hand mirrors'; sᵉḏînîm 'fine linen garments'; ṣᵉnîp̄ôṯ 'turbans'; rᵉḏîḏîm 'veils'. 3:24 ḥăḡôrāh 'girdle' (draft 'sash' changed); nip̄qāh 'rope'; maʿăśeh miqšeh 'well-set hair'; pᵉṯîḡîl 'robe'; MT kî (noun) 'branding'. Uncertain identifications and the alternatives (sun-discs, lunar amulets, amulet cases, armlets, garments of gauze, foreheads, 1QIsaᵃ 'shame') are reported in commentary only.
entries.rationale: The catalogue of Isa 3:18-23 is the longest list of women's dress and jewellery in the Hebrew Bible, and many of its twenty-one items occur only here, so their identification depends on etymology, later Hebrew, cognate languages and the ancient versions, and remains uncertain for several (Wildberger, Isaiah 1-12; Williamson, ICC Isaiah 1-5, 2006; Platt, AUSS 17, 1979). The Editor's rule is to give each item the conventional rendering best supported by that evidence, to give each Hebrew word its own English word (so the three draft collisions are resolved: 'headbands' for šᵉḇîsîm replaces the opaque 'cauls'; 'scarves' for rᵉʿālôṯ replaces the archaic 'mufflers' and frees 'veils' for rᵉḏîḏîm; 'girdle' for ḥăḡôrāh in 3:24 avoids a clash with qiššurîm 'sashes' and keeps the root ḥgr audible in maḥăḡōreṯ 'girding'), and to say in commentary where the identification is open. Where two readings are both defensible the established one is kept in the line: 'hand mirrors' (Vulgate) over 'garments of gauze' (Old Greek) at 3:23, 'ankle chains' (from ṣʿd 'step') over 'armlets' at 3:20, 'perfume boxes' over 'amulet cases' at 3:20, 'secret parts' over 'foreheads' (Akkadian pūtu) at 3:17. Astral or magical identifications, the 'little suns' of šᵉḇîsîm and the protective lunar function of the śahărōnîm, are reported in commentary and labelled as interpretation; they are not carried in the line. At 3:24 the Masoretic noun kî 'branding' is kept and the 1QIsaᵃ plus 'shame' reported (mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah). Every rendering is a standard one, so the entry is direct; the uncertainty is lexical, not a matter of the project lens.

entries.translit: mašʿēn ûmašʿēnāh; ḥăḵam ḥărāšîm; nᵉśûʾ p̄ānîm; taʿălûlîm; yiśśāʾ; ḥōḇēš; kāšᵉlāh; hakkāraṯ pᵉnêhem; ʾôy lᵉnap̄šām; ʾôy; mᵉʿôlēl; billēʿû; biʿartem; gᵉḇûrāṯēḵ; wᵉniqqāṯāh
entries.lemma: single-site lexical decisions of Isaiah 3 outside the finery oracle
entries.literal: support (m.) and support (f.); wise of crafts; lifted of face; caprices/babes; he lifts; binder; she stumbled; the recognising of their faces; woe to their soul; acting as child; they swallowed; you grazed; your might; she is emptied
entries.standardEnglish: stay and staff / support and staff; cunning artificer / skilful magician; honorable man / dignitary; babes; lift up (his voice) / cry out; healer; is ruined / has stumbled; the show of their countenance / their partiality; woe unto their soul; children; destroy / confuse; eaten up / devoured; thy mighty; desolate / ravaged
entries.wohChoice: 3:1 'support and staff' (merism in commentary); 3:3 ḥăḵam ḥărāšîm 'the expert craftsman' ('magician' in commentary); nᵉśûʾ p̄ānîm 'the man of rank' (draft 'the honored man' changed, to keep it distinct from nikbāḏ 'the honored', 3:5); 3:4 'babes'; 3:7 'lift up his voice' (object supplied), ḥōḇēš 'a healer'; 3:8 'has stumbled' (pun on makšēlāh 3:6); 3:9 'the look of their faces' ('partiality' in commentary), 'Woe to their soul!' (nep̄eš 'soul', the Isaiah default; ʾôy 'Woe' as for hôy); 3:11 ʾôy 'Woe'; 3:12 mᵉʿôlēl 'children' (Masoretic reading; singular participle rendered as a collective), billēʿû 'have destroyed' ('confused' in commentary); 3:14 biʿartem 'have eaten up' (bʿr 'graze', not 'burn'); 3:25 'your mighty'; 3:26 'emptied'.
entries.rationale: Each item is a site where the Translator flagged a choice between a standard rendering and a defensible alternative. The Editor keeps the draft wherever it gives the established sense of the Masoretic Text and records the alternative in commentary, so the text carries no reading that a Hebraist would contest: 'expert craftsman' follows the Masoretic vowels of ḥărāšîm (plural of ḥārāš, cf. 2 Kgs 24:14, 16) over the homonym ḥereš 'magic'; 'children' follows the Masoretic reading of mᵉʿôlēl (homonym ʿll II 'act as a child'; both homonyms fit the same Poel vowels) over the Old Greek's 'glean' (ʿll 'deal severely, glean', Lam 1:22; 2:20); 'has eaten up' takes bʿr in its grazing sense (Exod 22:4; Isa 5:5), which distinguishes it from bʿr 'burn' at 6:13 (levaer-massevet-stump-isaiah). Only one line changes: nᵉśûʾ p̄ānîm becomes 'the man of rank' (2 Kgs 5:1; Isa 9:14), because the draft gave 'honored' to two different Hebrew words in 3:3 and 3:5. The nep̄eš rendering 'soul' follows the signed-off Isaiah chapters (15:4; 26:9; 29:8; 44:20) and is not applied where nep̄eš is part of an object name (3:20, under daughters-of-zion-finery-isaiah-3). The interjection ʾôy is rendered 'Woe', consistent with the wave ruling for hôy. All choices are standard renderings, so the entry is direct. Wave I-3 (Isa 9): the same lexical decisions govern two later sites, so they are extended here rather than duplicated (one entry per lexical decision). At 9:14 nᵉśûʾ p̄ānîm is 'the man of rank', as at 3:3 (ASV 'the honorable man'). At 9:15 the wording of 3:12 recurs (mᵉʾaššᵉrê … maṯʿîm ûmᵉʾuššārāyw mᵉḇullāʿîm), and the line again takes 'those who lead' and blʿ 'destroyed', with blʿ II 'confused' (NRSV) in commentary. The tense differs from 3:12 ('led them astray … were destroyed') because of the poem's tense ruling (poem-tense-outstretched-hand-isaiah-9). If the orchestrator folds the per-chapter lexical-cruxes-isaiah-N entries into one book-level entry, as the wave I-1 sign-off package contemplates, these two refIds go with the 3:3 and 3:12 items.

entries.strongs: H6780 (ṣemaḥ); H6529 (pᵉrî); H776 (ʾereṣ); H8597 (tip̄ʾereṯ)
entries.lemma: ṣemaḥ; pᵉrî; ʾereṣ; tip̄ʾereṯ
entries.literal: the sprout/growth of YHWH; the fruit of the land
entries.standardEnglish: the branch of the LORD (ASV, NRSV); the Branch of the LORD (KJV-tradition capitalised, NIV); the fruit of the land; excellent and comely (ASV, lᵉ-predicates as adjectives)
entries.wohChoice: 'the branch of YHWH' in lower case, 'the fruit of the land'; the four lᵉ-predicates kept as nouns ('beauty and glory … pride and honor'), with tip̄ʾereṯ 'honor' so that 'splendor' stays reserved for hāḏār (overlay `hadar-splendor-isaiah`) and 'glory' for kāḇôḏ. The royal ṣemaḥ of Jer 23:5; 33:15 and the name 'Branch' of Zech 3:8; 6:12 and the Targum's 'the Messiah of YHWH' are reported in commentary, not imposed by capitalisation.
entries.rationale: ṣemaḥ is 'sprout, growth', what springs from the ground (BDB 855; HALOT 1034; Gen 19:25; Ezek 16:7; Ps 65:11), and in 4:2 it stands in synonymous parallel with pᵉrî hāʾāreṣ 'the fruit of the land', which favours the vegetation reading: the restored growth of the land as YHWH's gift to the survivors (Wildberger, Isaiah 1-12, 1991; Williamson, Isaiah 1-5, ICC 2006; Blenkinsopp, Isaiah 1-39, AB 19, 2000). The messianic reading rests on the Targum ('the Messiah of YHWH'; defended by Oswalt, The Book of Isaiah 1-39, NICOT 1986) and on the later royal usage: in Jer 23:5; 33:15 the title is ṣemaḥ ṣaddîq lᵉḏāwiḏ 'a righteous branch for David', with David as the genitive, and in Zech 3:8; 6:12 'Branch' is a name ('my servant the Branch', 'a man whose name is Branch'); none of these has the construct ṣemaḥ YHWH, so the title cannot simply be read back into Isa 4:2. Capitalising 'Branch' would decide between the two readings in the English, which the Hebrew does not do; the lower case keeps ASV and NRSV and leaves the question to the commentary. ʾereṣ in pᵉrî hāʾāreṣ is the land of Israel (Num 13:20, 26; Deut 1:25), not the cosmic earth of overlay `eretz-cosmic-scope-isaiah-24`, which stays scoped to ch. 24. The lᵉ-predicates (li-ṣḇî û-lᵉḵāḇôḏ … lᵉḡāʾôn û-lᵉṯip̄ʾereṯ) are rendered as nouns, the literal grammar, where ASV smooths them into adjectives; bare kāḇôḏ is the standard 'glory'. tip̄ʾereṯ ('beauty, glory, honour', BDB 802; HALOT) is rendered 'honor', its sense in the triad 'for praise, for fame and for honor' (Deut 26:19; Jer 13:11), because the wave I-1 overlay entry `hadar-splendor-isaiah` reserves 'splendor' for hāḏār (2:10, 19, 21; 53:2) and 'beauty' is ṣᵉḇî in the same verse; the change is a concordance fix. The signed-off 13:19 already renders tip̄ʾereṯ 'splendor' ('the splendor of the pride of the Chaldeans'), which the orchestrator should reconcile with `hadar-splendor-isaiah`.
