entries.translit: ʿānān yômām wᵉʿāšān wᵉnōḡah ʾēš lehāḇāh lāylāh; ḥuppāh; mᵉḵôn; miqrāʾehā; sukkāh
entries.strongs: H6051 (ʿānān); H6227 (ʿāšān); H5051 (nōḡah); H784 (ʾēš); H3852 (lehāḇāh); H2646 (ḥuppāh); H4349 (māḵôn); H4744 (miqrāʾ); H5521 (sukkāh)
entries.lemma: ʿānān; ʿāšān; nōḡah; ḥuppāh; māḵôn; miqrāʾ; sukkāh
entries.literal: cloud by day and smoke, and brightness of fire of flame by night; canopy / bridal chamber; fixed place; convocations; booth
entries.standardEnglish: a cloud and smoke by day, and the shining of a flaming fire by night … over all the glory shall be spread a covering (ASV); a pavilion (ASV); habitation; assemblies
entries.wohChoice: 4:5 'a cloud by day and smoke, and the shining of a flaming fire by night' (Hebrew order, divided at the zaqef on wᵉʿāšān); ḥuppāh 'a canopy' (NRSV, NJPS; replacing ASV 'covering'), with the ASV construal 'for over all the glory there shall be a canopy'; mᵉḵôn 'habitation' and miqrāʾehā 'her assemblies' (ASV, MT). 4:6 sukkāh 'a pavilion' (ASV, NJPS). No 'pillar' is supplied; the verse is governed for its Exodus relation by central `pillar-of-cloud-and-fire-ammud-ha-anan-ve-esh-divine-presence-marker-cross-corpus`.
entries.rationale: ḥuppāh is 'canopy' at Isa 4:5 and 'bridal chamber' at Joel 2:16 and Ps 19:6 [Eng. 5] (HALOT 323; BDB 342), and 'canopy' is the modern standard (NRSV, NJPS), so the line replaces ASV's vaguer 'covering' with the lexical core of the word, a change of precision, not of reading. The construal of kî ʿal-kol-kāḇôḏ ḥuppāh is open: the glory may be what the canopy shelters, or the canopy itself ('over everything the glory shall be a canopy'); the line keeps ASV's 'over all the glory' and records the alternative in commentary. In the day/night sequence the Masoretic accents put the disjunctive zaqef on wᵉʿāšān, so cloud and smoke form the day sign and the shining fire the night sign; the line keeps the Hebrew word order (against ASV's regrouping 'a cloud and smoke by day') and lets the punctuation follow the accents. The vocabulary is plain theophany language (ʿānān, ʿāšān, ʾēš, as at Exod 13:21-22; 19:18), and since the verse has no ʿammûḏ the line supplies no 'pillar'; the Exodus relation and the disavowal apparatus belong to the central pillar entry. mᵉḵôn is the fixed place of YHWH's dwelling (Exod 15:17; 1 Kgs 8:13) and ASV 'habitation' is kept; miqrāʾehā 'her assemblies' (Lev 23:2-4) is kept against the LXX's 'all the places around it' under overlay `mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`. sukkāh is a booth of branches (1:8; Lev 23:42; central `sukkot-toponym-and-festival-etymology` governs only the toponym and plural), but at 4:6 it is the divine shelter of v. 5, and ASV/NJPS 'pavilion' is kept rather than the field-hut 'booth' of 1:8.

entries.strongs: H7121 (qārāʾ); H8034 (šēm); H622 (ʾāsap̄); H2781 (ḥerpāh); H6413 (pᵉlêṭāh); H7604 (šāʾar); H3498 (yāṯar); H3789 (kāṯaḇ); H2416 (ḥay); H6675 (ṣōʾāh); H1818 (dām); H4941 (mišpāṭ); H1197 (bāʿar)
entries.lemma: single-site lexical decisions of Isaiah 4:1-4
entries.literal: let your name be called over us, gather up our reproach; escaped remnant of; the one left … the one remaining; the one written for/among the living; excrement of; bloods of; judgment; burning / purging
entries.standardEnglish: let us be called by thy name; to take away our reproach (ASV); them that are escaped (ASV); he that is left … he that remaineth; every one that is written among the living (ASV); filth; blood; justice (ASV) / judgment (KJV, NRSV); burning
entries.wohChoice: 4:1 'only let us be called by your name — take away our reproach' (ASV sense; the literal 'let your name be called over us' in commentary). 4:2 pᵉlêṭaṯ yiśrāʾēl 'the survivors of Israel'. 4:3 'whoever is left … whoever remains'; 'everyone who is written among the living' (ASV; 'recorded for life' in commentary). 4:4 ṣōʾāh 'filth', dᵉmê 'the blood', mišpāṭ 'justice' (ASV), bāʿēr 'burning'.
entries.rationale: Each item is a single-site decision where the draft's ASV-based wording is a defensible standard rendering, and the Editor keeps it while recording the alternative in commentary. (1) yiqqārēʾ šimḵā ʿālênû is the formula of ownership and protection (2 Sam 12:28; Isa 63:19), and ASV/NRSV 'let us be called by your name' gives its sense in idiomatic English; ʾsp ḥerpāh 'take away reproach' is the phrase of Gen 30:23 (central `yosef-double-name-aetiology`, cited, not extended, since its wohChoice governs the Joseph naming speeches). (2) pᵉlêṭaṯ yiśrāʾēl is the collective sense of pᵉlêṭāh (2 Kgs 19:30-31 = Isa 37:31-32), so 'the survivors of Israel' (NRSV) is used; central `pleitah-deliverance-escape-remnant-tradition-cross-corpus` names the collective sense but its wohChoice is the event sense 'a great deliverance' (Gen 45:7), so it is cited, not extended. (3) han-nišʾār and han-nôṯār are participles, not the noun šᵉʾērîṯ governed by central `she-erit-remnant-cross-corpus-theological-keyword`, which is therefore cited, not extended; kāṯûḇ la-ḥayyîm is ambiguous between the civic register 'among the living' (ASV; Ezek 13:9; Neh 7:5) and the book-of-life 'for life' (NRSV, NJPS; Exod 32:32-33; Ps 69:29; Dan 12:1), and the line keeps ASV because the Hebrew does not decide. (4) ṣōʾāh is literally excrement (Deut 23:14; Isa 28:8), for which 'filth' is the standard English; dᵉmê, a plural of shed blood, is 'the blood' (ASV); mišpāṭ is kept as ASV 'justice' with 'judgment' (KJV, NRSV) recorded; bāʿēr is 'burning' (bʿr, BDB 128-129; HALOT 145), with the purge sense of the Deuteronomic ûḇiʿartā (Deut 13:6) recorded, for which NJPS 'a spirit of purging' is a witness.

entries.source: וַיְקַו לְמִשְׁפָּט וְהִנֵּה מִשְׂפָּח לִצְדָקָה וְהִנֵּה צְעָקָה
entries.translit: wayqaw lᵉmišpāṭ wᵉhinnēh miśpāḥ, liṣḏāqāh wᵉhinnēh ṣᵉʿāqāh
entries.strongs: H4941 (mišpāṭ); H4939 (miśpāḥ); H6666 (ṣᵉḏāqāh); H6818 (ṣᵉʿāqāh)
entries.lemma: מִשְׂפָּח
entries.literal: he waited for justice, and behold, [miśpāḥ]; for righteousness, and behold, a cry
entries.standardEnglish: he looked for justice, but, behold, oppression; for righteousness, but, behold, a cry (ASV)
entries.wohChoice: 'he waited for justice, but behold, bloodshed; for righteousness, but behold, an outcry' — miśpāḥ 'bloodshed' (BDB; NRSV); ṣᵉʿāqāh 'an outcry' under the central zaaqah-outcry-of-the-oppressed entry. Presentation rule: the paronomasia (mišpāṭ/miśpāḥ, ṣᵉḏāqāh/ṣᵉʿāqāh) is NOT reproduced in the line, either by parenthetical transliteration or by a sound-echo; it is explained in commentary.
entries.rationale: מִשְׂפָּח occurs only here, and its meaning has to be recovered from etymology and from the pun. BDB places it under a root 'pour out' (cf. Arabic safaḥa 'shed blood') with the sense 'outpouring (of blood), bloodshed', the value NRSV adopts; ASV 'oppression' and JPS 1917 'violence' give the general sense the context requires without a lexical basis. The Editor adopts 'bloodshed' because it has the etymological support, it matches the forensic cry of victims in the parallel ṣᵉʿāqāh (the blood that 'cries out', ṣōʿăqîm, Gen 4:10), and it echoes the hands 'full of blood' of Isa 1:15; because the derivation is not certain, the claim is inferred rather than direct. On presentation: the Translator's draft placed the four transliterations in parentheses in the line, which has almost no precedent in the corpus and turns the verse into an apparatus. Sound-echoes such as NJPS 'justice … injustice; equity … iniquity' keep the pun but change the meaning of both second terms, which accuracy-before-lens rules out. The line therefore carries the plain meanings and the commentary on 5:7 states the pun with the Hebrew forms (Wildberger, Isaiah 1-12, 1991; Williamson, ICC Isaiah 1-5, 2006). The split pair mišpāṭ/ṣᵉḏāqāh is rendered 'justice'/'righteousness' but is not placed under the central tzedakah-u-mishpat-justice-pair entry, following the 32:16 split-pair precedent of wave I2.

entries.strongs: H7337 (rḥb, Hiphil); H7585 (šᵉʾôl); H5315 (nep̄eš)
entries.lemma: נֶפֶשׁ
entries.partOfSpeech: verb + noun (nep̄eš in its physical sense)
entries.literal: She'ol has made wide its throat
entries.standardEnglish: Sheol hath enlarged her desire (ASV)
entries.wohChoice: 'She'ol has widened its throat' — nep̄eš in its physical sense 'throat, gullet', parallel to pîhā 'its mouth'.
entries.rationale: נֶפֶשׁ has 'throat, gullet' as a basic physical sense alongside 'appetite, life, self' (HALOT nepeš 1; cf. Ps 69:2; Jonah 2:6), and the parallel colon 'and opened its mouth beyond measure' fixes that sense here. NJPS renders 'gullet' and the same idiom of a widened nep̄eš describes insatiable greed at Hab 2:5 ('who widens his nep̄eš like She'ol'). ASV 'enlarged her desire' abstracts the image into appetite and loses the anatomical parallelism the verse builds. The Editor therefore renders 'widened its throat'; the sense is lexicon-attested and adopted by a major modern version, so the claim is direct. The central nefesh-blessing-transfer entry (Gen 27, nep̄eš as agent of blessing, transliterated) has a different register and is deliberately not applied; the Ugaritic parallel of Mot's devouring jaws (KTU 1.5 II 2-4) is noted in commentary only.

entries.strongs: H1197 (bʿr; Strong's does not separate the homonyms)
entries.lemma: בָּעַר II
entries.partOfSpeech: verb, Piel infinitive construct with lᵉ
entries.literal: and it shall be for grazing / for being browsed
entries.standardEnglish: it shall be eaten up (ASV); it shall be devoured (NRSV)
entries.wohChoice: 'it shall be eaten up' (ASV) — bʿr II 'graze, browse', paired with lᵉmirmās 'for trampling'. The 6:13 entry levaer-massevet-stump-isaiah (bʿr I 'for burning') does not govern this site.
entries.rationale: The same form לְבָעֵר is rendered 'for burning' at 6:13 under levaer-massevet-stump-isaiah, whose rationale records 'be browsed' as a minority construal there. In 5:5 the context decides the other way: the hedge is removed so that the vineyard is opened to animals, and the parallel colon has lᵉmirmās 'for trampling', which points to the homonym bʿr II 'graze, browse' (HALOT; cf. the Hiphil of livestock grazing a field, Exod 22:4). ASV 'eaten up', NRSV 'devoured' and the standard commentaries read it so (Wildberger, Isaiah 1-12; Williamson, ICC Isaiah 1-5). A separate entry is made, rather than a context clause in the 6:13 entry, because the lexicons treat the two as distinct roots, and recording the split keeps the two renderings of one written form auditable. The rendering is the standard one and carries no lens.

entries.source: בְּכָל־זֹאת לֹא־שָׁב אַפּוֹ וְעוֹד יָדוֹ נְטוּיָה
entries.translit: bᵉḵol-zōʾṯ lōʾ-šāḇ ʾappô wᵉʿôḏ yāḏô nᵉṭûyāh
entries.strongs: H7725 (šûḇ); H639 (ʾap); H3027 (yāḏ); H5186 (nāṭāh)
entries.lemma: refrain formula
entries.partOfSpeech: refrain (verbal clause + nominal clause with passive participle)
entries.literal: in all this his nose/anger has not turned, and still his hand is stretched out
entries.standardEnglish: For all this his anger is not turned away, but his hand is stretched out still (ASV)
entries.wohChoice: 'For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still' — fixed wording for every occurrence of the refrain (5:25; Heb. 9:11, 16, 20; 10:4).
entries.rationale: The refrain closes 5:25 and each strophe of the poem of 9:7-10:4 (Heb. 9:11, 16, 20; 10:4; Eng. 9:12, 17, 21; 10:4), and many commentators hold that 5:25-30 belongs with that poem (Wildberger, Isaiah 1-12; Blenkinsopp, Isaiah 1-39, AB 19, 2000; Williamson). One fixed English wording is needed so that the repetition stays visible across chapters. šûḇ with ʾap as subject is the idiom for anger subsiding (Gen 27:44-45; Hos 14:5), for which English 'turn away' is the established equivalent (ASV, NRSV); the Translator's 'turned back' is literal but not idiomatic. lōʾ-šāḇ is rendered as a perfect, 'has not turned away', because the strokes the poem lists have already fallen, and the waw of wᵉʿôḏ is rendered 'and' rather than ASV's interpretive 'but'. The rendering is standard and carries no lens. Forward scope: when chapters 9-10 are drafted, ISA-9:11, ISA-9:16, ISA-9:20 and ISA-10:4 (Hebrew versification, the corpus refId basis) should be added to appliesTo and rendered identically. Wave I-3 (Isa 10): the refrain at 10:4 is rendered in the fixed wording, unchanged from the draft. The first half of the verse (the biltî crux) is governed by lexical-cruxes-isaiah-10.

entries.source: שְׁאָר יָשׁוּב (7:3; as a clause 10:21); עִמָּנוּ אֵל (7:14; 8:8; as a clause כִּי עִמָּנוּ אֵל 8:10); מַהֵר שָׁלָל חָשׁ בַּז (8:1, 3)
entries.translit: šᵉʾār yāšûḇ; ʿimmānû ʾēl; mahēr šālāl ḥāš baz
entries.strongs: H7610 (Šᵉʾār Yāšûḇ); H6005 (ʿImmānûʾēl); H4122 (Mahēr Šālāl Ḥāš Baz); components H7605 (šᵉʾār), H7725 (šûḇ), H5973 (ʿim), H410 (ʾēl). Strong's numbers from recall, not concordance-verified.
entries.lemma: the sentence-names of Isaiah 7-8, given to children as signs (8:18)
entries.partOfSpeech: personal names formed from clauses; at 8:10 and 10:21 the same words used as clauses
entries.literal: 'a remnant will return'; 'with us (is) God'; 'the spoil hastens, the plunder speeds' (or imperative 'hasten the spoil, hurry the plunder')
entries.standardEnglish: ASV, NRSV and NJPS transliterate Shear-jashub (7:3), Immanuel (7:14; 8:8) and Maher-shalal-hash-baz (8:1, 3); ASV 8:8 'O Immanuel'; ASV 8:10 'for God is with us'; ASV 10:21 'A remnant shall return'
entries.wohChoice: Transliterated names in the line, with the meaning given in commentary: 'Shear-jashub' (7:3), 'Immanuel' (7:14), 'Maher-shalal-hash-baz' (8:1, 3); at 8:8 the vocative 'O Immanuel'. Where the same words function as a clause they are translated: 8:10 kî ʿimmānû ʾēl 'for God is with us' (commentary links 7:14 and 8:8); 10:21 šᵉʾār yāšûḇ 'A remnant will return' (commentary notes the echo of 7:3). The name-meaning is never inserted into the line in brackets, and the line does not decide whether šûḇ is 'come back' or 'turn back' (repent).
entries.rationale: Isaiah 7-8 gives three children names that are whole sentences, and 8:18 says that the prophet and his children are 'signs and portents in Israel', so the names carry the message of the chapters. English translations agree in transliterating them as names (ASV, NRSV, NJPS), and the Editor follows that practice because a translated name ('A-remnant-will-return your son') reads as a clause and hides the fact that the Hebrew is a personal name. Where the same words are not a name but a clause, the Hebrew syntax changes and the translation must change with it: kî ʿimmānû ʾēl at 8:10 is the reason clause closing an oracle against the nations, and šᵉʾār yāšûḇ at 10:21 is the subject and verb of a sentence followed by an apposition ('the remnant of Jacob'). Rendering them as clauses there, while the commentary draws the links back to 7:3 and 7:14, lets the reader see both the name and its meaning without importing a translation into the name sites. The meanings themselves are not in doubt, but their force is: šᵉʾār yāšûḇ can be threat ('only a remnant') or promise, and šûḇ can be return or repentance, so the commentary sets out both and the line stays neutral. ʾēl in the clause at 8:10 is 'God' under elohim-el-eloah-monotheistic-formula-isaiah; that entry is not applied to the name sites because the name is transliterated. The noun šᵉʾār is distinct from šᵉʾērîṯ, so the central she-erit-remnant-cross-corpus-theological-keyword (whose rationale cites the name) is not applied to the line. Chapter 8 sites (wave I-3 ruling 1): Maher-shalal-hash-baz transliterated at 8:1 (with lᵉ- 'For', ASV and NJPS; 'Belonging to' in commentary) and 8:3 (ASV hyphenation), its meaning ('the spoil speeds, the prey hastens'; JPS 1917 translates it at 8:1, verified) in commentary; 8:8 'O Immanuel', vocative, with ASV, KJV and JPS 1917, the clause reading of NJPS ('But with us is God, whose wings are spread', verified) and of the Septuagint (not verified) recorded in commentary; 8:10 kî ʿimmānû ʾēl as the clause 'for God is with us' (ASV, JPS 1917), with the link to 7:14 and 8:8 drawn in commentary. Wave I-3 (Isa 10): at 10:21 and 10:22 šᵉʾār yāšûḇ is a clause, 'A remnant will return' (10:21) and 'only a remnant of them will return' (10:22, with bô), not the transliterated name. The commentary notes that the verses unfold the meaning of the name Shear-jashub (7:3), and that yāšûḇ can mean 'return' or 'turn back, repent'. The plain noun šᵉʾār 'remnant' (10:19, 20, 21b) is ASV and needs no entry.

entries.strongs: H5959 (ʿalmâ); contrast H1330 (bᵉṯûlâ). Strong's numbers from recall, not concordance-verified.
entries.lemma: ʿalmâ 'young woman (of marriageable age)', feminine of ʿelem 'young man'
entries.partOfSpeech: noun (feminine singular) with the definite article
entries.literal: the young woman
entries.standardEnglish: ASV and KJV 'a virgin' (following the Greek hē parthenos as cited in Matt 1:23); RSV 'a young woman'; NRSV and NJPS 'the young woman'
entries.wohChoice: 'Behold, the young woman is with child and shall bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel' (ISA-7:14). ʿalmâ 'young woman', with the article kept ('the'); hārâ as the adjective 'is with child'; yōleḏeṯ as a participle 'shall bear'; wᵉqārāʾṯ as 'and shall call', subject the young woman. The identity of the woman is not decided in the line. The Septuagint's parthenos and its reception in Matt 1:23 are given in commentary and are governed for the Matthew line by the central isa-7-14-virgin-birth-mt-1-22-23-parthenos-vs-almah-philological-dispute-cross-corpus, which is NOT applied to the Hebrew line. Any Wheel of Heaven reading appears only in a labelled speculative paragraph of the commentary.
entries.rationale: ʿalmâ is the feminine of ʿelem 'young man' (1 Sam 17:56; 20:22) and denotes a young woman of marriageable age; the standard lexica (BDB, HALOT) do not give it the specific sense 'virgin', which is the sense bᵉṯûlâ usually carries (Lev 21:13-14; Deut 22:23-29); BDB's gloss for ʿalmâ is 'young woman (ripe sexually; maid or newly married)'. The other occurrences (Gen 24:43; Exod 2:8; Ps 68:26 Heb.; Prov 30:19; Song 1:3; 6:8) are consistent with that sense, and the Editor's rendering matches the modern scholarly translations (RSV, NRSV, NJPS); the claim is therefore direct. The Hebrew has the definite article, so the line says 'the young woman' rather than RSV's 'a young woman'. The departure from ASV's 'a virgin' is the most visible in the book, and it is made because ASV here follows the rendering of the Greek text cited in Matt 1:23 rather than the Hebrew, which the project's accuracy-above-lens rule does not allow for a Hebrew line. Two points are recorded so the decision is auditable rather than polemical: bᵉṯûlâ itself is sometimes qualified (Gen 24:16; Joel 1:8), and it is often observed that no biblical ʿalmâ is clearly a married woman; the line renders what the word denotes and does not claim what it excludes. The tense pattern follows the grammar of the annunciation formula shared with Gen 16:11 and Judg 13:5, and the subject of qārāʾṯ follows the 3fs reading because no woman is addressed in the verse; the Septuagint's second-person kaléseis 'you shall call' is verified and reported, and the 1QIsaᵃ reading reported as wqrʾ is disclosed as not verified. The project's Matthew 1:23 line follows the Septuagint that Matthew cites, under the central entry, so the two lines differ by design: each translates its own source.

entries.strongs: H758 (ʾĂrām). Strong's numbers from recall, not concordance-verified.
entries.lemma: ʾărām, the Aramean kingdom of Damascus and its people
entries.literal: Aram
entries.standardEnglish: ASV 'Syria', 'the Syrians' (after the Greek and Latin tradition); NRSV and NJPS 'Aram', 'the Arameans'
entries.wohChoice: 'Aram' for the state or land and for the people as a collective subject (7:1, 2, 4, 5, 8; 9:11); 'the Arameans' where the Hebrew uses a gentilic or plural form. Never 'Syria' or 'the Syrians'. Wave I-3 ruling 4 also fixes the English forms Ephraim, Manasseh, Egypt and Assyria; other place names take the ASV spelling unless a glossary entry fixes another form.
entries.rationale: The Hebrew name of the kingdom ruled from Damascus is ʾărām, and the modern scholarly translations (NRSV, NJPS) print 'Aram'. ASV's 'Syria' comes from the Greek and Latin versions, which used the later geographical name, and it now suggests the modern state to most readers. The 1 Kings translation in the corpus already prints 'Aram' (e.g. 1 Kgs 22), so this entry brings Isaiah into line with the corpus and with the Hebrew. In Isaiah 7 the name stands both for the kingdom (7:1, 8) and for its people or army as a collective subject (7:2, 5), and the line uses 'Aram' for both, as NRSV does. The ruling is book-wide (also 17:3 when drafted) and carries no interpretive weight beyond the name.

entries.strongs: H6973 (qûṣ I 'feel loathing, dread'). Strong's numbers from recall, not concordance-verified.
entries.lemma: qûṣ I 'feel a loathing or dread'; Hiphil 'cause dread'
entries.partOfSpeech: verb: Hiphil imperfect cohortative 1cp with 3fs suffix (7:6); Qal participle or perfect 2ms (7:16)
entries.literal: 7:6 'and let us cause it dread'; 7:16 'you feel dread before'
entries.standardEnglish: ASV 'vex it' (7:6), 'whom thou abhorrest' (7:16); NRSV 'cut off Judah' (7:6), 'dread' (7:16)
entries.wohChoice: 7:6 'and terrify it'; 7:16 'whose two kings you dread'. The two sites are rendered with the vocabulary of dread so that the reader can see the root recur: the coalition plans to put Judah in dread, and Ahaz is in dread of the coalition.
entries.rationale: At 7:16 the sense is secure: qûṣ with mippᵉnê means 'be in dread of', as in Exod 1:12 (the Egyptians in dread of the Israelites) and Num 22:3 (Moab in dread of Israel), so ASV's 'abhor' gives the wrong emotion and is replaced by 'dread'. At 7:6 the form nᵉqîṣennāh is disputed. BDB gives the Hiphil of the same root, 'let us cause her sickening dread', but calls that parse weak and recommends reading nᵉṣîqennāh, from ṣûq 'distress, press hard'; others derive the form from a root meaning 'cut, tear apart' (NRSV 'cut off Judah'). The Editor keeps the qûṣ parse, which both the parse and the ṣûq emendation support in sense (pressure and terror), because the same root is then used in the same chapter for the two sides of the crisis, and because the following verb (nabqiʿennāh 'let us break into it') supplies the military action without needing a second verb of violence. Because the 7:6 derivation is not certain, the entry is marked inferred; the 7:16 rendering on its own would be direct.

entries.strongs: H8319 (šāraq). Strong's numbers from recall, not concordance-verified.
entries.lemma: šāraq 'whistle, hiss'
entries.literal: to whistle / to hiss
entries.standardEnglish: ASV 'hiss' (5:26; 7:18); NRSV and NJPS 'whistle'
entries.wohChoice: Context decides. 'whistle (for)' where šāraq + lᵉ- is a signal that summons (5:26 'and whistle for them'; 7:18 'YHWH will whistle for the fly … and for the bee'). 'hiss' where it expresses scorn or horror at a ruin (e.g. Jer 19:8; Lam 2:15; 1 Kgs 9:8), when those texts are drafted.
entries.rationale: šāraq names the sound made through pursed lips, and English needs two words for its two uses. With lᵉ- 'for' it is a call that brings someone, as a beekeeper or herdsman calls; the image in 7:18, of YHWH calling the fly and the bee, depends on that sense, and NRSV and NJPS render 'whistle'. In the ruin formulas (Jer 19:8; Lam 2:15) the same verb is the sound of scorn, where 'hiss' is right. ASV uses 'hiss' at 5:26 and 7:18 as well, which in modern English suggests contempt and misreports a summons. The wave I-1 line at 5:26 already prints 'whistle', and this entry records the decision for both Isaiah sites so they stay concordant.

entries.source: Isaiah 7 (various): וְלֹא יָכֹל (7:1); נָחָה … עַל (7:2); זַנְבוֹת הָאוּדִים (7:4); טָבְאַל (7:6); תַאֲמִינוּ / תֵאָמֵנוּ (7:9); שְׁאָלָה (7:11); אֲנָשִׁים (7:13); הָרָה וְיֹלֶדֶת … וְקָרָאת; אוֹת (7:14); חֶמְאָה (7:15, 22); לְדַעְתּוֹ (7:15); בַּתּוֹת, נַעֲצוּצִים, נַהֲלֹלִים (7:19); תַּעַר הַשְּׂכִירָה, שַׂעַר הָרַגְלָיִם (7:20); לֹא־תָבוֹא … יִרְאַת; מַעְדֵּר (7:25)
entries.strongs: H3201 (yāḵōl); H5117 (nûaḥ); H2180 (zānāḇ); H181 (ʾûḏ); H2870 (Ṭāḇᵉʾēl); H539 (ʾāman); H7592 (šāʾal); H582 (ʾĕnôš); H2030 (hārâ); H3205 (yālaḏ); H7121 (qārāʾ); H226 (ʾôṯ); H2529 (ḥemʾâ); H1327 (battâ); H5285 (naʿăṣûṣ); H5097 (nahălōl); H8593 (taʿar); H7917 (śᵉḵîrâ); H4576 (maʿdēr). Strong's numbers from recall, not concordance-verified.
entries.lemma: the smaller lexical and syntactic decisions of Isaiah 7 not given their own entry
entries.literal: see wohChoice
entries.standardEnglish: ASV throughout, except where stated
entries.wohChoice: 7:1 'but could not prevail against it' (ASV; MT singular yāḵōl vs 2 Kgs 16:5 plural, in commentary). 7:2 'Aram is confederate with Ephraim' (ASV sense; literal 'has settled upon' in commentary). 7:4 'these two tails of smoking firebrands' (ASV). 7:6 'the son of Tabeel' (conventional name; MT ṭāḇᵉʾal explained in commentary as a pausal form or as a 'good-for-nothing' pun, the two alternatives BDB gives). 7:9 'If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established' (ASV; kî asseverative; the ʾmn root-play explained, not imitated). 7:11 MT pointing šᵉʾālāh 'ask it' (ASV); the Sheol repointing in commentary. 7:13 halʾôṯ ʾănāšîm 'to weary people' (ASV and NJPS 'men'; NRSV 'mortals'), the generic plural rendered without a gendered English word in line with wave I-1 decision 2, option C1 (founder ruling 2026-11-26); not a site of the ʾāḏām / ʾîš refrain, so adam-humankind-ish-man-isaiah does not govern it. 7:14 'a sign' for ʾôṯ; the tense and subject of the annunciation formula as in almah-young-woman-isaiah-7-14. 7:15, 22 ḥemʾâ 'curds' (replacing ASV 'butter'); 7:15 lᵉḏaʿtô 'when he knows' (ASV). 7:19 'desolate valleys … thorn-hedges … pastures' (ASV); nāḥû 'settle' (ASV 'rest'). 7:20 'a razor that is hired … the hair of the feet … consume' (ASV; the euphemism kept, not explained, in the line). 7:25 'you shall not come there for fear of briers and thorns' (ASV, 2ms construal; the NJPS 3fs construal in commentary); bammaʿdēr yēʿāḏērûn 'hoed with the hoe' (as 5:6 'hoed').
entries.rationale: These decisions are collected in one entry, following the per-chapter practice of wave I-1, because each governs a single site or a single pair of sites and would bloat the overlay as separate entries. Most ratify the Translator's ASV default and are recorded only so that the commentary's alternatives are auditable. The one lexical change is ḥemʾâ: the word denotes curdled or soured milk (BDB 'curd'; NRSV, NJPS 'curds'), and ASV's 'butter' gives a modern product in place of the biblical one, so 'curds' is printed at 7:15 and twice at 7:22. Two decisions are made for concordance with wave I-1 lines: 'hoed' at 7:25 matches yēʿāḏēr at 5:6, and 'settle' at 7:19 keeps the verb of 7:2 recognisable in English. Where the Masoretic Text is kept against an emendation or a repointing (7:8, 7:11, 7:17, 7:20) the policy is mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah, not this entry. One line follows a wave I-1 ruling rather than the ASV: at 7:13 ʾănāšîm is a generic plural set against 'my God', and 'people' replaces ASV 'men' because wave I-1 decision 2, option C1 (founder ruling 2026-11-26), avoids gendered English words for generic human nouns. The site is outside the ʾāḏām / ʾîš refrain governed by adam-humankind-ish-man-isaiah, so the decision is recorded here.

entries.translit: hāʾōḇôṯ wᵉhayyiddᵉʿōnîm (sg. ʾôḇ; yiddᵉʿōnî) (8:19); kᵉʾôḇ mē-ʾereṣ (29:4)
entries.strongs: H178 (ʾôḇ); H3049 (yiddᵉʿōnî). Strong's numbers from model recall, not concordance-verified.
entries.lemma: ʾôḇ 'spirit of the dead; one who calls it up'; yiddᵉʿōnî 'knowing (spirit); one who consults it' (from ydʿ 'know')
entries.partOfSpeech: nouns (fem. pl. ʾōḇôṯ, masc. pl. yiddᵉʿōnîm), articular, as objects of dāraš ʾel 'seek, consult'
entries.literal: the ʾôḇ-spirits and the knowing ones
entries.standardEnglish: them that have familiar spirits and … the wizards (ASV, KJV); the ghosts and the familiar spirits (JPS 1917; NJPS 'the ghosts and familiar spirits'); NRSV 'the ghosts and the familiar spirits' (not verified)
entries.wohChoice: 'the ghosts and the familiar spirits' at 8:19 ('Seek the ghosts and the familiar spirits that chirp and mutter'): the pair rendered as the spirits consulted, not as the practitioners, because the following participles hamᵉṣap̄ṣᵉp̄îm wᵉhammahgîm describe their voices. Context rule for later sites of the pair in Isaiah (19:3): 'the ghosts' / 'the familiar spirits' where the consulted spirits are meant; 'mediums' / 'necromancers' only where the context requires persons, with a note. No etymological rendering ('the knowing ones') in the line. ʾôḇ alone in the simile kᵉʾôḇ mē-ʾereṣ at 29:4 is 'a ghost' ('your voice will be like that of a ghost from the ground'), governed by this entry (moved from ariel-ob-isaiah-29, founder ruling 2026-11-26); at 29:4 the verb ṣpṣp is rendered 'whisper' ('your speech will whisper'), where 8:19 has 'chirp' for its participle.
entries.rationale: ʾôḇ and yiddᵉʿōnî are the paired terms of the Hebrew Bible's necromancy vocabulary (Lev 19:31; 20:6, 27; Deut 18:11; 1 Sam 28:3, 9; 2 Kgs 21:6; 23:24; Isa 19:3). Both can denote either the spirit of the dead that is consulted or the person who consults it: Lev 20:27 speaks of a man or woman 'in whom is' an ʾôḇ or yiddᵉʿōnî, while 1 Sam 28:3 has Saul remove them from the land (BDB; HALOT; Tropper, DDD s.v. 'Spirit of the dead'; not verified). At Isa 8:19 the spirits are meant: the articular participles 'that chirp and that mutter' describe the faint voices of the dead, as the voice of the ghost 'chirps' (tᵉṣap̄ṣēp̄) from the dust at 29:4. JPS 1917 and NJPS (both verified on Sefaria) render 'the ghosts and the familiar spirits', and NRSV is reported to do the same; ASV's 'them that have familiar spirits … the wizards' renders practitioners and loses the link between the nouns and the participles. 'Ghost' also keeps 8:19 consistent with 29:4, where the overlay already renders ʾôḇ 'a ghost'. 'Familiar spirit' is kept for yiddᵉʿōnî because it is the established English term for this word in all three versions; the objection recorded at 29:4 (that the phrase suggests a witch's animal companion) was made against using it for ʾôḇ, and the pairing with 'ghosts' makes the sense plain here. No central entry covers either term (central v2.93.0 searched by id, source, wohChoice, rationale and appliesTo for Lev 19:31, 20:6, 27, Deut 18:11, 1 Sam 28, 2 Kgs 21:6, 23:24); the entry is placed in the overlay and should be promoted to central when Leviticus 19-20, Deuteronomy 18 or 1 Samuel 28 is translated. The rendering is the standard modern one and carries no lens, so the claim is direct. Housekeeping (founder ruling 2026-11-26): ISA-29:4 is moved here from ariel-ob-isaiah-29, which now governs only the Ariel sites (29:1, 2, 7), so that ʾôḇ 'ghost' is governed by one entry in the book. The reasons for 'a ghost' at 29:4 carry over: ASV's 'one that hath a familiar spirit' is an archaism that modern readers take to mean a witch's companion animal, and NRSV and NJPS have 'a ghost'. At 29:4 the line renders the verb ṣpṣp 'whisper' ('from the dust your speech will whisper'), while 8:19 has 'chirp' for the participle hamᵉṣap̄ṣᵉp̄îm; the two English verbs are not harmonised in this wave, and the difference is an open item for the next revision of either chapter.

entries.literal: with a stylus of a man; and he/it shall go up … his/its wings; shout (?) … be shattered; as with strength of the hand; attestation; for signs and for tokens; dawn; and he shall pass through it … and curse by his king; driven out; he made light … he made heavy
entries.standardEnglish: with the pen of a man / in common script; it … its (ASV) / he … his (KJV, JPS 1917); make an uproar (ASV) / band together (NJPS); with a strong hand (ASV) / took me by the hand (NJPS); testimony (ASV) / message (NJPS); signs and wonders (ASV) / signs and portents (NJPS); morning (ASV) / dawn (NJPS); they … their (ASV) / he … his (NJPS); driven away (ASV); made glorious (ASV) / dealt a more grievous blow (JPS 1917)
entries.wohChoice: 8:1 'a large tablet … with the pen of a man' (ASV literal; 'in common script' in commentary); 8:7-8 masculine pronouns kept as 'he … his' (KJV, JPS 1917; River or king left open), kᵉḇôḏô 'his glory' under the wave concordance; 8:9 rōʿû 'Make an uproar' (rwʿ), wāḥōttû 'be shattered', merḥaqqê-ʾāreṣ under eretz-cosmic-scope-isaiah-24; 8:11 'with a strong hand, and instructed me' (MT ysr); 8:16, 20 tᵉʿûḏāh 'testimony' in both verses, tôrāh 'teaching' under torah-teaching-isaiah, 8:16 the imperatives are the prophet's, because the line closes YHWH's speech at the end of 8:15 (house style lower-cases divine pronouns, so 'my disciples' does not itself decide the speaker); 8:18 'for signs and for wonders' (as Deut 4:34 in the project's Torah; portent sense in commentary); 8:20 'To the teaching and to the testimony!' as exclamation, šaḥar 'dawn'; 8:21 plural 'they … their' for the singular collective, qillēl bᵉ- 'curse by'; 8:22 'into thick darkness they shall be driven away' (mᵉnuddāḥ Pual participle); 8:23 'In the former time he brought into contempt … but in the latter time he has made it glorious' (ASV reversal reading). 8:19b-21 construal (A), the prophet's reply, is kept (founder ruling 2026-11-26); the continued quotation of JPS 1917 and NJPS, with ʾĕlōhîm as the dead (NJPS 'its divine beings'), is reported in commentary at 8:19-21 and not printed.
entries.rationale: Each item is a site where the Translator flagged a choice between the ASV rendering and a defensible alternative. The Editor keeps the established sense of the Masoretic Text in every case and records the alternatives in commentary; no item adopts an emendation and none carries a project reading. The checks are these: ASV 1901 was verified against its text (it has 'it … its' at 8:7-8, not 'he … his' as the draft reported, so the line's 'he … his' rests on KJV and JPS 1917, both verified, and leaves the River/king referent open as the Hebrew masculine does); JPS 1917 and NJPS were verified on Sefaria, including NJPS 'Band together' (8:9), 'took me by the hand' (8:11), 'message' (8:16), 'signs and portents' (8:18) and the persons reading of 8:23, and JPS 1917's judgment reading of hiḵbîḏ at 8:23 ('dealt a more grievous blow'), a construal discussed in Emerton, JSS 14 (1969) 151-175 (bibliographic details verified via Crossref; his conclusion not checked). 'Signs and wonders' is kept at 8:18, against NJPS 'portents', because the project renders the same pair 'signs … wonders' at Deut 4:34 and the pair should stay recognisable across the corpus; the sense of môp̄ēṯ as an ominous token is explained in commentary. 'Testimony' is kept for tᵉʿûḏāh at both 8:16 and 8:20 so that the repeated pair is visible. At 8:23 the reversal reading (contempt, then glory) is kept because it is the standard construal of hēqal/hiḵbîḏ in the major English versions and lexica (BDB kbd Hiphil 'make honourable'; not verified); its reuse at Matt 4:15-16 is noted in commentary and is not the reason for the choice. The kāḇôḏ of 8:7 is the Assyrian king's array, so the divine-glory entries are not applied; 'glory' follows the wave concordance. The entry may be folded into a wave-level crux entry at merge. Post-review (wave I-3 Reviewer): the 8:20 exclamation item goes with construal (A) of 8:19, which rests on ASV and KJV and was confirmed by founder ruling 2026-11-26; JPS 1917 and NJPS both continue the quotation through 8:20a, and that reading is reported in commentary.

entries.strongs: H410 (ʾēl); H1368 (gibbôr)
entries.lemma: אֵל + גִּבּוֹר
entries.partOfSpeech: noun + adjective/noun (divine epithet; one of the throne names at 9:5)
entries.literal: God, a mighty one / a warrior
entries.standardEnglish: Mighty God (ASV, NRSV; NJPS within its sentence-name 'The Mighty God is planning grace'); alternatives proposed by some commentators (not verified): 'God is a warrior' (sentence-name), 'mighty hero' (ʾēl as adjective)
entries.wohChoice: 'Mighty God' at 9:5 (third throne name) and 10:21 ('to the Mighty God'); capitalised 'God' as for ʾēl designating the deity. The alternatives 'God is a warrior' and 'mighty hero' are recorded in commentary only.
entries.rationale: ʾēl gibbôr is rendered 'Mighty God' by ASV, NRSV and NJPS, and the rendering is the standard one; NJPS keeps 'The Mighty God' as the subject of its sentence-name ('The Mighty God is planning grace'). The decisive in-book evidence is 10:21, where the same two words name the God to whom the remnant of Jacob returns (šᵉʾār yāšûḇ … ʾel-ʾēl gibbôr), so there ʾēl can only be the deity; the book should render the phrase the same way at both sites. The same epithet stands in the Deuteronomic formula hāʾēl haggāḏōl haggibbōr (Deut 10:17; cf. Jer 32:18; Neh 9:32). Two alternatives are serious and are recorded in commentary: a theophoric sentence-name, 'God is a warrior', on the model of Isaiah's other sign-names (7:3; 7:14; 8:3), proposed by some commentators (not verified by the Reviewer); and ʾēl as an adjective 'mighty', 'mighty hero', supported by ʾêlê gibbôrîm 'the mighty among the warriors' (Ezek 32:21). Neither is preferred to the standard reading, and 10:21 tells against the adjectival one. The overlay entry elohim-el-eloah-monotheistic-formula-isaiah is not applied: its scope is the incomparability and denial formulas of Isaiah 13 and 40-48. The capital follows the same practice, 'God' for ʾēl denoting the deity. Whether the title, given to a Davidic king, makes a claim about the king's nature is a question for commentary and reception, not for the line. Strong's numbers from recall; not concordance-verified. Wave I-3 extension (Isa 10): ʾel-ʾēl gibbôr at 10:21 is rendered 'to the Mighty God', capitalised as at 9:5 (Eng. 9:6), so that the repetition of the throne name is visible. At 10:21 the phrase unambiguously designates YHWH (compare hāʾēl haggāḏōl haggibbōr, Deut 10:17; Jer 32:18). The commentary refers the alternatives ('God is a warrior', 'mighty hero') to this entry.

entries.lemma: the birth announcement and throne names of Isa 9:5, with miśrāh at 9:5-6
entries.partOfSpeech: verbal clauses (Pual and Niphal perfects; wayyiqtol forms) + a sequence of nominal names
entries.literal: for a child has been born to us, a son has been given to us, and the rule has come to be upon his shoulder, and one has called his name wonder-counselor, God-warrior, father-of-perpetuity, prince-of-peace
entries.standardEnglish: For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder; and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace (ASV); For a child has been born for us, a son given to us; authority rests upon his shoulders; and he is named Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace (NRSV); He has been named 'The Mighty God is planning grace; The Eternal Father, a peaceable ruler' (NJPS, footnote 'As in 25.1')
entries.wohChoice: 'For a child has been born to us, a son has been given to us; and the government has come upon his shoulder; and he has been named Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.' Tense: perfects and wayyiqtol forms as English perfects. Names: four paired titles, 'Wonderful Counselor', following the pashta/zaqef grouping of the accents (the lowest-level telisha division, which ASV follows, is recorded in commentary). miśrāh 'the government' at 9:5 and 9:6 (ASV; 'authority' NRSV/NJPS in commentary).
entries.rationale: Two decisions depart from ASV, and both rest on the Hebrew. First, tense: yullaḏ and nittan are perfects and wattᵉhî and wayyiqrāʾ are wayyiqtol forms. ASV's 'is born … shall be … shall be called' reads them as prophetic perfects of a future birth. NRSV ('has been born … rests … is named') and NJPS render them as completed events, as does the accession-oracle analysis (Alt 1950; von Rad 1947). The English perfect reports the forms without settling whether the event is the birth of an heir or an enthronement, and v. 6's taʿăśeh 'will do' carries the future. wayyiqrāʾ is active with an indefinite subject, rendered by the English passive 'he has been named'. Second, the names: in the accent hierarchy the zaqef on gibbôr splits the sequence into two halves, the pashta on yôʿēṣ groups peleʾ yôʿēṣ against ʾēl gibbôr, and the tipcha separates ʾăḇîʿaḏ from śar-šālôm; only at the lowest level does the telisha gedolah separate peleʾ from yôʿēṣ, and ASV and KJV follow that division with five names. The line pairs them as 'Wonderful Counselor' (NRSV), because the other three names are two-word units, because peleʾ yôʿēṣ reads naturally as 'a wonder of a counselor', and because 28:29 applies the same roots to YHWH (hip̄lîʾ ʿēṣāh). Isaiah 25:1 joins the same roots again (peleʾ ʿēṣôṯ), and NJPS cross-references it here. The pairing agrees with the higher-level accent grouping and is held by many modern commentators (Wildberger, Isaiah 1-12, 1991; Roberts, First Isaiah, Hermeneia, 2015; both cited from memory). It departs from the traditional English, so the entry is inferred. miśrāh occurs only at 9:5-6 and comes from śrr 'rule', the root of śar in 'Prince of Peace'. ASV 'government' is kept and 'authority' is recorded in commentary. NJPS reads a sentence-name in two halves that follow the zaqef division: 'The Mighty God is planning grace; The Eternal Father, a peaceable ruler' (footnote 'As in 25.1'); it is reported in commentary. Reception readings (LXX 'messenger of great counsel', the Targum's messianic gloss, b. Sanh. 94a on Hezekiah, Luke 1:32-33, and a labelled speculative Wheel of Heaven note) stay in commentary.

entries.lemma: tense of the narrated strokes in the poem of the outstretched hand, Isa 9:7-20
entries.partOfSpeech: verbal system (wayyiqtol, weqatal, yiqtol and participles in narrative sequence)
entries.literal: and he raised high … and they devoured … and he cut off … and they were … and it kindled … and they rolled up … and it was … and he cut … and he ate
entries.standardEnglish: ASV mixed futures and presents ('will set up … shall devour … will cut off … are destroyed … is the land burnt'); NRSV past throughout ('raised … devoured … cut off … led them astray … was burned'); NJPS mixed (past at 9:8 'noted', 9:10 'let … triumph', 9:17-19; future at 9:13 'will cut off' and 9:16 'Will not spare'); JPS 1917 future/present throughout
entries.wohChoice: Past throughout the strokes of 9:7-20: wayyiqtol forms as English simple past; the imperfects and participles inside each stroke (9:10 yᵉsaksēḵ; 9:16 lōʾ yiśmaḥ, lōʾ yᵉraḥēm, dōḇēr; 9:17 tōʾḵēl; 9:18 yaḥmōlû; 9:19 yōʾḵēlû) and the weqatal frame verbs of 9:7-8 (wᵉnāp̄al, wᵉyāḏᵉʿû) take the past of their context; the negated perfects of a continuing state (9:12) and the fixed refrain (9:11, 16, 20) as English perfects; the quoted boast of 9:9 keeps its own tenses; the nominal clauses of 9:14 as present. Waw-consecutive 'So' (9:10, 13); ʿal-kēn 'Therefore' (9:16). Does not bind the separate woe-oracle 10:1-4 beyond its refrain.
entries.rationale: The poem narrates each stroke with wayyiqtol forms, the Hebrew past narrative, and a single tense policy is needed so that the four strophes read as one review of judgments already suffered. The grammatical default for these forms is past, and NRSV renders the strokes so. The book has already rendered the narrative verbs of 5:25, which most commentators assign to this poem (Wildberger; Blenkinsopp, AB 19, 2000; Williamson), as past, and the wave I-1 refrain entry renders lōʾ-šāḇ 'has not turned away' on the ground that the strokes have already fallen. ASV's futures follow the older reading of the poem as forecast. That reading treats the waw-consecutive as converted to the future, which the forms do not support in this context. The ruling is inferred rather than direct because it extends the past to the imperfects, participles and weqatal forms inside each stroke. In a past narrative chain those forms can express past circumstance or repetition, but they do not require it. Two sites are soft points: 9:8 wᵉyāḏᵉʿû, where a future ('shall know', ASV, JPS 1917) remains possible, and 9:16, where ʿal-kēn + yiqtol is rendered future by NJPS ('Will not spare'). NJPS is itself mixed, with past at 9:8, 9:10 and 9:17-19 and future at 9:13 and 9:16, which confirms that the ruling is a reading, not a grammatical necessity. Both soft points are reported in commentary. The quoted speech of 9:9 and the explanatory nominal clauses of 9:14 are outside the narrative and keep their own tenses. The chapter 10 oracle (10:1-4) is a separate woe-oracle and is not governed by this entry except for the refrain at 10:4.

entries.lemma: single-site lexical and textual decisions of Isaiah 9
entries.partOfSpeech: nouns, verbs, participles and prepositional phrases
entries.literal: boot of the booted one; a word … in Jacob; adversaries of Rezin; from before … from behind; godless; folly; he does not rejoice; rising of smoke; [hapax]; he cut; the flesh of his arm; Manasseh [object] Ephraim
entries.standardEnglish: ASV: armor of the armed man; sent a word into Jacob; the adversaries of Rezin; before … behind; profane; folly; shall have no joy; mount up in the lifting up of smoke; is the land burnt up; snatch; the flesh of his own arm; Manasseh, Ephraim (no verb). NRSV: boots of the tramping warriors; against Jacob; adversaries against them; east … west; godless; folly; did not have pity; column of smoke; was burned; gorged; flesh of their kindred; Manasseh devoured Ephraim
entries.wohChoice: 9:4 'every boot of the one who tramps in the tumult' (BDB; NRSV); 9:7 MT dāḇār 'a word', 'sent … against Jacob'; 9:10 MT 'the adversaries of Rezin' kept (emendations ṣārāyw / śārê in commentary); 9:11 'Aram from the east and the Philistines from the west' (NRSV sense; 'Aram' per wave ruling; cf. 2:6 miqqeḏem 'from the east'); 9:16 ḥānēp̄ 'godless' (wave ruling; 32:6), nᵉḇālāh 'folly' (ASV; 32:6), MT lōʾ-yiśmaḥ 'did not rejoice' (1QIsaᵃ variant in commentary); 9:17 gēʾûṯ ʿāšān 'a column of smoke'; 9:18 neʿtam 'was burnt up' (ASV; hapax); 9:19 wayyiḡzōr 'snatched' (ASV), MT 'the flesh of his own arm' (emendation rēʿô in commentary); 9:20 verb 'devoured' supplied from 9:19, English forms 'Manasseh', 'Ephraim'.
entries.rationale: Each item is a site where the Translator flagged a choice between standard renderings. The Editor keeps the Masoretic text throughout and departs from ASV only where a lexicon or the context requires it. (1) sᵉʾôn and its denominative participle are related by BDB to Akkadian šēnu 'shoe, sandal', so 'boot' (NRSV) replaces ASV's lexically unsupported 'armor'. (2) At 9:7 MT dāḇār is kept against the reported Old Greek 'death' (deḇer); that reading was not verified against Ziegler and is given only in commentary. šālaḥ bᵉ- is hostile in this context ('against', NRSV), as the parallel 'fell on Israel' shows. (3) At 9:10 the difficult ṣārê rᵉṣîn is kept and the emendations are reported. (4) miqqeḏem / mēʾāḥôr has both the 'front/back' and the 'east/west' sense, and the compass reading fits the geography of Aram and Philistia and the book's own 2:6. (5) ḥānēp̄ 'godless' and nᵉḇālāh 'folly' follow the stable 32:6 (wave ruling 5). The central nevalah entry is not applied, because its subject is the communal-outrage formula, not speech. The 1QIsaᵃ variant behind NRSV 'did not have pity' is reported without verification (DJD 32 not held). (6) gēʾûṯ is the rising of smoke (gʾh), distinct from gāʾôn 'majesty' in the book's concordance. (7) neʿtam is a hapax with no secure etymology; ASV's 'burnt up' fits the fire imagery and is kept, with the alternatives in commentary. (8) gzr 'cut' is rendered by its contextual sense 'snatched' (ASV). MT zᵉrōʿô is kept against the emendation rēʿô (NRSV). (9) At 9:20 the object markers require the verb of 9:19. NRSV supplies it, and the line supplies 'devoured' so that the verse does not read as a list. The proper names take English forms (wave ruling 4), and the Genesis-scoped central menasheh-name-aetiology-tribe ('Menasheh') is not applied. All the choices are standard renderings in at least one major version or lexicon, so the entry is direct; the uncertain items are disclosed in commentary.

entries.strongs: H6757 (from recall; not concordance-verified)
entries.lemma: צַלְמָוֶת
entries.partOfSpeech: noun (feminine/abstract form; Masoretic pointing as a compound)
entries.literal: deep darkness (ṣlm 'be dark' + abstract ending); by the Masoretic analysis 'shadow of death' (ṣēl + māwet)
entries.standardEnglish: the shadow of death (ASV, KJV); deep darkness (NRSV); gloom (NJPS, 'a land of gloom')
entries.wohChoice: 'deep darkness' ('in the land of deep darkness', 9:1); the compound analysis 'shadow of death' and its reception (Ps 23:4 KJV; Matt 4:16) in commentary.
entries.rationale: This entry splits out the lexeme decision that the central sha-arei-mavet records in its rationale for Job 38:17, where it is attached to the 'gates' phrase (orchestrator ruling, wave I-3). Most modern lexica derive ṣalmāwet from ṣlm 'be dark', cognate with Akkadian ṣalāmu 'be black', with an abstract ending (HALOT; BDB records both analyses). The Masoretic vocalisation with -māwet reflects the older compound ṣēl 'shadow' + māwet 'death', which the ancient versions and the KJV/ASV tradition follow. At Isa 9:1 the word stands in parallel with ḥōšeḵ 'darkness', and nothing in the verse concerns death, so 'deep darkness' (NRSV) gives the sense that the context and the lexica support; NJPS 'gloom' has the same sense. Because the rendering matches the modern lexical consensus and a major version, the claim is direct. The traditional rendering is kept visible in commentary. If later Isaiah sites or other books adopt the same decision, the orchestrator may promote the entry to a central lexeme entry.

entries.lemma: single-site lexical decisions of Isaiah 10
entries.literal: decrees of iniquity … trouble; day of visitation; desolation; your weight/glory; except crouch under; rod / staff; a godless nation; spoil / plunder; her images; the boasting of the height of his eyes; like a mighty one, the sitting ones; leanness; as the melting of a sick one; escaped remnant; righteousness; their wearing-out; because of fat; a lodging they lodged; by a mighty one
entries.standardEnglish: unrighteous decrees … perverseness (ASV) / oppressive statutes (NRSV); the day of visitation (ASV) / punishment (NRSV); desolation (ASV) / calamity (NRSV); your glory (ASV) / wealth (NRSV); they shall only bow down under the prisoners (ASV); rod / staff; a profane nation (ASV); spoil / prey (ASV); her idols (ASV) / images (NRSV); the glory of his high looks (ASV); like a valiant man … them that sit on thrones (ASV); leanness (ASV); as when a standard-bearer fainteth (ASV) / as when an invalid wastes away (NRSV); they that are escaped (ASV); righteousness; their destruction; by reason of fatness (ASV) / because of the anointing (KJV); they have taken up their lodging (ASV); by a mighty one (ASV)
entries.wohChoice: 10:1 'iniquitous decrees … the writers who write mischief' (ʿāmāl 'mischief', over ASV 'perverseness'). 10:3 'the day of visitation … the desolation'; kāḇôḏ 'glory' at 10:3, 16, 18 under the strict wave rule, with the 'wealth' sense in commentary. 10:4 'Nothing remains but to crouch under the prisoners, and they shall fall under the slain' (biltî 'nothing but'; taḥaṯ 'under'; the sg./pl. shift kept). šēḇeṭ 'rod', maṭṭeh 'staff' throughout the chapter (10:5, 15, 24, 26; as 9:3); 10:5 construed with ASV. 10:6 gôy ḥānēp̄ 'a godless nation' (wave ruling 5). šālāl 'spoil' and baz/bzz 'plunder' (10:2, 6), one pair so that the echo of Maher-shalal-hash-baz (8:1, 3) stays visible. 10:11 ʿăṣabbîm 'images', distinct from ʾĕlîlîm 'idols' in the same verse. 10:12 tip̄ʾereṯ 'boasting' (recorded departure from the 'honor' default). 10:13 'like a valiant man … those who sit on thrones' (ASV). 10:16 rāzôn 'leanness among his fat ones' (ASV). 10:18 kimsōs nōsēs 'as when a sick man wastes away'. 10:20 pᵉlêṭaṯ 'the survivors' (as 4:2). 10:22 ṣᵉḏāqāh 'righteousness'. 10:25 'their destruction' (MT plural suffix). 10:27 šemen 'fatness' (MT). 10:29 'they have taken up their lodging at Geba' (narrative reading, ASV and JPS 1917; NJPS's quoted speech 'Geba is to be our night quarters!' in commentary). 10:34 'by a mighty one' (agent unspecified).
entries.rationale: Each item is a single-site decision that keeps a standard rendering, chosen between ASV and NRSV on lexical grounds, and records the alternative in commentary. None carries a project reading. (1) ʿāmāl is 'trouble, mischief, toil' (BDB), and 'perverseness' (ASV) is not a sense of the noun. 'Mischief' keeps the word's own meaning, whereas NRSV's 'oppressive statutes' paraphrases the clause. (2) biltî is the particle 'except, nothing but' (BDB). The line gives its sense in the modern idiom ('Nothing remains but …'), keeps the Masoretic shift from singular kāraʿ to plural yippōlû, and renders taḥaṯ by its basic 'under'. Lagarde's Beltis/Osiris redivision is reported and not adopted, under `mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah`. (3) šēḇeṭ 'rod' and maṭṭeh 'staff' are fixed for the chapter so that the instrument imagery of 10:5, 15, 24 and 26 stays traceable, as at 9:3. (4) ḥānēp̄ follows wave I-3 ruling 5 ('godless'; NRSV), so that it matches the stable 32:6 'godlessness'. (5) Two different idol-nouns stand in parallel at 10:11, and the line now distinguishes them ('idols … images', with NRSV); ʾĕlîlîm stays under central `elilim-idols-cross-corpus`. (6) At 10:12 tip̄ʾereṯ is pejorative, 'vaunting, pomp', and the wave default 'honor' (4:2) would invert its sense in this idiom. Wave I-3 ruling 6 allows a recorded departure, and 'boasting' ties the noun to the Hithpael yiṯpāʾēr 'boast itself' of the same root at 10:15. (7) At 10:18 the pair mᵉsōs nōsēs is derived from māsas 'melt' and a root nss 'be sick, waste away', as the lexicons give it, with NRSV. ASV's 'standard-bearer' rests on a derivation from nēs 'banner' that is now rarely followed, so accuracy decides against the ASV wording. (8) At 10:29 lānû may be the verb 'they lodged' (lyn/lûn) or the preposition 'for us' introducing quoted speech. The accentuation does not decide between them, because the suffixed preposition is also stressed on the first syllable (WLC 9:5; 1:9). The line keeps the narrative reading of ASV and JPS 1917 (NRSV likewise, from memory), and the commentary reports NJPS's quoted-speech reading 'Geba is to be our night quarters!'. (9) At 10:27 šemen is rendered 'fatness' (MT; ASV). KJV 'the anointing' and the NRSV emendation 'from Rimmon' are reported in commentary. Putting 'anointing' in the line would read a cultic sense into a noun that the context of animal imagery does not require. (10) The remaining items (10:3, 13, 16, 20, 22, 25, 34) keep ASV or the corpus wording already fixed at 4:2, with the NRSV alternatives given in commentary.

entries.lemma: place names of Isaiah 10:9 and the march itinerary 10:28-32
entries.literal: the Hebrew place names; baṯ-gallîm 'daughter of Gallim'
entries.standardEnglish: ASV: Calno, Carchemish, Hamath, Arpad, Aiath, Migron, Michmash, Geba, Ramah, Gibeah of Saul, Gallim, Laishah, Anathoth, Madmenah, Gebim, Nob; NRSV largely the same; scholarly transliteration (Kalno, Karkemish, ʿAyyat, Mikmas) in some commentaries
entries.wohChoice: ASV spellings for every toponym of the chapter (wave I-3 ruling 4: place names take the ASV spelling unless an entry fixes another form), with English forms for Samaria, Damascus, Jerusalem, Zion, Egypt, Assyria, Midian and Lebanon. No site is identified in the line beyond the Hebrew name: identifications (Aiath with Ai; Laishah as Laish with directional -āh; the Michmash pass of 1 Sam 13:23; 14:4) and the debated historical occasion of the march stay in commentary. baṯ-gallîm 'O daughter of Gallim' keeps the personification, as 'the daughter of Zion' (1:8). madmēnāh at 10:31 is the town and is not governed by `madmenah-ketiv-qere-moab-isaiah-25`.
entries.rationale: The glossary had no Isaiah toponym convention, and the itinerary of 10:28-32 depends on its names being recognisable to a reader who checks a map or a standard Bible. ASV spellings are those of the corpus baseline and differ from NRSV only marginally, so the choice is a house-style decision, not an interpretation. A scholarly transliteration was considered and rejected for the line because it would set this chapter apart from the rest of the corpus. The Hebrew form is given in commentary wherever the identification matters (ʿayyaṯ, layᵉšāh). The route the names trace (Ai, Michmash, Geba, Ramah, Gibeah, Anathoth, Nob) is a well-known approach to Jerusalem from the north, through Benjamin. Its historical occasion is disputed (an Assyrian advance often tied to 701 BCE, the Syro-Ephraimite campaign of about 734 BCE, or a literary itinerary; see Wildberger, Isaiah 1-12; Blenkinsopp, Isaiah 1-39, AB 19; Sweeney, Isaiah 1-39, FOTL 16). The line therefore names no army and decides nothing. Keeping the identification out of the line means a later archaeological or textual ruling changes only commentary.

entries.translit: ḥōṭer mig-gezaʿ yišāy wᵉnēṣer miš-šārāšāyw yip̄reh
entries.strongs: H2415 (ḥōṭer); H1503 (gezaʿ); H5342 (nēṣer); H8328 (šōreš); H6509 (pārāh 'bear fruit'). Strong's numbers from model recall, not concordance-verified.
entries.lemma: ḥōṭer 'shoot, rod'; gezaʿ 'stock, stem, stump'; nēṣer 'sprout, offshoot'
entries.literal: a shoot from the stock of Jesse, and an offshoot from his roots shall bear fruit
entries.standardEnglish: a shoot out of the stock of Jesse, and a branch out of his roots shall bear fruit (ASV); a twig shall grow forth out of his roots (JPS 1917); a shoot … out of the stump of Jesse, a twig shall sprout from his stock (NJPS)
entries.wohChoice: 'a shoot out of the stock of Jesse, and a twig out of his roots shall bear fruit' (11:1): ḥōṭer 'shoot', gezaʿ 'stock' (as at 40:24), nēṣer 'twig' (JPS 1917, NJPS). 'branch' is reserved for ṣemaḥ (4:2, overlay tsemach-yhwh-branch-isaiah-4) and 'stump' for maṣṣeḇeṯ (6:13). Lower case; the royal and messianic reception (Targum; Matt 2:23 'Nazarene') is reported in commentary only. MT yip̄reh 'shall bear fruit' kept (mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah). Book rule for nēṣer (founder ruling 2026-11-26): never 'branch'; 'twig' at 11:1, where ḥōṭer already has 'shoot'; the stable 14:19 'a loathed branch' is to be revised to 'a loathed shoot' at its next revision, and 60:21 nēṣer maṭṭāʿay follows ('shoot'). ISA-14:19 and ISA-60:21 are added to appliesTo when those lines are made.
entries.rationale: Isa 11:1 uses two growth words, ḥōṭer and nēṣer, and neither is the ṣemaḥ of 4:2. ḥōṭer occurs elsewhere only at Prov 14:3, where it is a rod or switch; nēṣer is a sprout or offshoot (BDB; HALOT; Isa 14:19; 60:21; Dan 11:7). ASV renders nēṣer 'branch', but JPS 1917 and NJPS render it 'twig', so the line follows a standard Jewish translation and keeps 'branch' for ṣemaḥ, the word that becomes the royal title in Jer 23:5; 33:15 and Zech 3:8; 6:12. Keeping the two lemmas apart in English lets a reader see that Isa 11:1 does not use the title-word, which is a fact about the Hebrew, not a reading of it. gezaʿ 'stock' follows ASV and JPS 1917 and matches the stable 40:24 'their stock'; NJPS 'stump' is recorded, and 'stump' stays with maṣṣeḇeṯ at 6:13. One inconsistency is known: the stable 14:19 renders nēṣer nitʿāḇ 'a loathed branch' (ASV 'an abominable branch'). By founder ruling 2026-11-26, 14:19 is to be revised to 'a loathed shoot' at its next revision, and 60:21 nēṣer maṭṭāʿay follows when chapter 60 is drafted, so that 'branch' stays with ṣemaḥ throughout the book. Neither site is in appliesTo until its line is made; chapter 14 is not edited in this wave. The verb yip̄reh is MT (prh 'bear fruit'); LXX anabēsetai and Vulgate ascendet presuppose 'come up / sprout' and are reported in commentary.

entries.translit: nēs (nāśāʾ nēs 'raise a signal'; lᵉnēs ʿammîm 'as a signal for the peoples')
entries.strongs: H5251. Strong's numbers from model recall, not concordance-verified.
entries.lemma: nēs 'pole, standard, banner, signal'
entries.literal: a pole / banner raised as a sign
entries.standardEnglish: ensign (ASV, JPS 1917); signal (NRSV at 5:26, not verified; NJPS at 11:12); standard (NJPS at 11:10)
entries.wohChoice: 'signal' for nēs as a raised pole or banner throughout Isaiah: 'raise a signal for the nations' (5:26; 11:12), 'On a bare mountain raise a signal' (13:2), 'who stands as a signal for the peoples' (11:10); the same rendering is expected at the later banner sites (18:3; 30:17; 31:9; 49:22; 62:10). Exception: at 33:23 nēs is a ship's sail ('they could not spread the sail'), as at Ezek 27:7, and is rendered 'sail' there. ASV 'ensign' is not used.
entries.rationale: nēs is a pole or banner set up on a height to rally troops or people (BDB; HALOT; Num 21:8-9, where it is the pole of the bronze serpent; Jer 4:6; 51:12). ASV 'ensign' now suggests a naval flag or a rank to most readers, while 'signal' gives the function, which is what the Isaiah contexts turn on: in 5:26 YHWH raises it to summon a foreign army, in 13:2 it calls the host against Babylon, and in 11:10, 12 it gathers the nations and the dispersed of Israel. NJPS uses 'signal' at 11:12 and 'standard' at 11:10 (both checked against the NJPS text on Sefaria); the book already prints 'signal' at 5:26 (wave I-1) and in the signed-off 13:2, so the entry records an existing book practice rather than introducing a new one. One English word for the banner sense keeps the reversal between 5:26 and 11:10-12 visible to an English reader; the commentary notes it. The entry carries no project reading. The lemma also has a second, nautical sense: at Isa 33:23 and Ezek 27:7 nēs is the sail of a ship (BDB), and 'signal' would misreport it, so the entry excepts that site (added at the wave I-3 review).

entries.lemma: single-site lexical decisions of Isaiah 11
entries.literal: his smelling; and the fatling together; light-hole(?); stretched out(?); his resting place, glory; his hand, to acquire; the coastlands of the sea; the harassers of Judah; on the shoulder; the stretching-out of their hand; with the heat(?) of his wind; in sandals; counsel and might
entries.standardEnglish: ASV throughout; alternatives from JPS 1917 and NJPS recorded in commentary
entries.wohChoice: 11:2 MT's six qualities in three pairs, ʿēṣāh 'counsel', gᵉḇûrāh 'might' (ASV; LXX 'piety' and the seven-gifts tradition in commentary). 11:3 'his delight shall be in the fear of YHWH' (ASV, JPS 1917; literal 'his smelling' and NJPS 'he shall sense the truth' in commentary). 11:6 the Masoretic verbless clause 'and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together' (1QIsaᵃ/LXX 'shall feed' in commentary); gār 'dwell'. 11:8 'the hole of the asp … the adder's den … put his hand' (ASV). 11:10 mᵉnuḥāṯô kāḇôḏ 'his resting place shall be glory' (predicate noun kept, kāḇôḏ = 'glory'). 11:11 supplied 'set' (ASV), liqnôṯ 'to recover', ʾiyyê hayyām 'the coastlands of the sea' (as 24:15). 11:13 'those who harass Judah' (ASV construal), 'harass' for both ṣrr forms. 11:14 'swoop down upon the shoulder of the Philistines', ASV verbal rendering of the closing nominal clauses. 11:15 baʿyām rûḥô 'with his scorching wind' (ASV), 'cause men to march over dryshod' (ASV, 'men' supplied).
entries.rationale: Each item is a site where the Hebrew is rare, elliptical or ambiguous, and the line keeps a standard rendering (ASV, usually shared by JPS 1917) while the commentary reports the alternatives, and three items depart from ASV wording. (a) 11:10: ASV and JPS 1917 turn the predicate noun kāḇôḏ into the adjective 'glorious' and NJPS has 'honored'; the line keeps the noun, 'his resting place shall be glory', because wave ruling 6 makes 'glory' for kāḇôḏ strict, the book renders other verbless kāḇôḏ clauses literally (6:3; 24:23), and a predicate noun of quality is ordinary Hebrew syntax. (b) 11:11: ʾiyyê hayyām is 'the coastlands of the sea', not ASV and JPS 1917 'the islands of the sea', for concordance with the stable 24:15 ('in the coastlands of the sea') and 42:4 ('the coastlands'); ʾî denotes coast and island alike (BDB), and the places meant are the Mediterranean shores and islands, which 'coastlands' covers. (c) 11:14: ʿwp is 'swoop down' for ASV and JPS 1917 'fly down'; the verb is 'to fly', and in context it is the descent of a bird of prey on its victim (NJPS 'pounce'), which 'swoop down' states without adding anything to the verb's sense. At 11:3 the Hiphil of rwḥ is 'smell, take in the scent' (Lev 26:31; Amos 5:21), and NJPS notes that the meaning is uncertain; the idiomatic 'delight' is the reading of ASV and JPS 1917 and is kept, with NJPS's 'sense the truth' and the proposed deletion as a dittography reported. At 11:6 MT has no verb for the third pair; NJPS records that 1QIsaᵃ and the LXX read 'shall feed', and the line keeps MT under mt-qere-textual-policy-isaiah. At 11:8 mᵉʾûraṯ and hāḏāh occur only here (NJPS: 'Meaning of Heb. uncertain'), so ASV's contextual 'den' and 'put' are kept. At 11:11 MT has no verb governing yāḏô; ASV's supplied 'set' is kept, and ʾiyyê hayyām follows the stable 24:15 'the coastlands of the sea' rather than ASV 'islands'. At 11:13 ṣōrᵉrê yᵉhûḏāh may be objective (Judah's enemies; ASV, JPS 1917) or subjective (NJPS 'Judah's harassment'); the ASV construal is kept and the subjective reading, which fits the verse's second half, is reported. At 11:14 kāṯēp̄ may be the topographic 'slope' (Josh 15:8-11; NJPS 'the back of Philistia'), and the closing clauses are nominal in Hebrew; ASV's rendering is kept. At 11:15 baʿyām is a hapax (NJPS 'might', 'Meaning of Heb. uncertain'), and ASV 'scorching' is kept; wᵉhiḏrîḵ ban-nᵉʿālîm is literally 'make (them) tread in sandals', and ASV's supplied object 'men' is kept and identified as supplied in commentary.

entries.strongs: H1348 (gēʾûṯ); cf. H1347 (gāʾôn), H1342 (gāʾāh). Numbers from recall, not concordance-verified.
entries.lemma: gēʾûṯ 'a rising up; majesty; pride', noun of the root gʾh 'rise, be high'
entries.literal: a rising, loftiness
entries.standardEnglish: ASV 'he hath done excellent things' (12:5); JPS 1917 and NJPS 'gloriously' (12:5); 'majesty' (Ps 93:1); 'pride' (Isa 28:1, 3)
entries.wohChoice: 'majesty / majestic' where gēʾûṯ is the majesty of YHWH or of his acts: 12:5 'he has done majestic things'; 26:10 'the majesty of YHWH' (stable, already so printed). Context clauses: 'pride' where gēʾûṯ is human arrogance (Isa 28:1, 3 'the crown of pride', when drafted); the physical sense 'rising, column' where it is the upward movement of smoke or sea (Isa 9:17 Heb. gēʾûṯ ʿāšān 'a column of smoke', as the chapter 9 draft prints it; cf. Ps 89:10). Never 'glory' or 'gloriously', which are reserved for kāḇôḏ.
entries.rationale: Gēʾûṯ belongs to the root gʾh 'rise, be high', the root of gāʾôn, which the book renders 'majesty' (24:14; 2:10, 19, 21 under hadar-splendor-isaiah). The lexica give it a physical sense 'rising' and the evaluative senses 'majesty' and 'pride' (BDB; HALOT). Of YHWH it is the majesty he wears (Ps 93:1), and the stable chapter 26:10 already prints 'the majesty of YHWH', so 'majestic' at 12:5 keeps the root concordant within the book. The usual renderings of 12:5 are ASV 'excellent things', in an older sense of 'excellent' ('surpassing') that modern English has lost, and JPS 1917 / NJPS 'gloriously' (both checked on Sefaria). 'Gloriously' would put on a gʾh-noun the English that wave rule 6 reserves strictly for kāḇôḏ. The clause also echoes gāʾōh gāʾāh, the cognate verb that opens the Song of the Sea (Exod 15:1, 21), the song quoted at Isa 12:2. 'Majesty' is a standard lexical gloss and carries no interpretive load, so the claim is direct. The pejorative and physical senses are recorded as context clauses so that one entry governs the lemma book-wide.

entries.lemma: single-site lexical and syntactic decisions of Isaiah 12
entries.partOfSpeech: mixed (verb forms, nominal clause, nouns, participles)
entries.literal: let your anger turn and you comfort me; God (is) my salvation / the God of my salvation; springs of the salvation; call on his name; cause to remember; made known; she who dwells (in) Zion
entries.standardEnglish: ASV throughout; JPS 1917 'proclaim his name', 'This is made known'; NJPS 'Your wrath has turned back', 'the God who gives me triumph', 'fountains of triumph', 'proclaim', 'declare', 'You who dwell in Zion'; NRSV 'royal Zion' (recalled, not verified)
entries.wohChoice: 12:1 a statement, 'your anger has turned away, and you comfort me' (ASV, JPS 1917, NJPS), against the strict jussive wish; the verb 'turn away' as in the refrain bekhol-zot-lo-shav-appo-refrain-isaiah, whose reversal the clause is. 12:2 nominal clause 'Behold, God is my salvation' (ASV, JPS 1917), with the NJPS construct noted. 12:3 'the wells of salvation' (ASV, JPS 1917), with the lexical sense 'springs / fountains' in commentary. 12:4 'call on his name' (central qara-b-shem-yhwh), 'make known his deeds among the peoples' (as in ASV Ps 105:1), 'make mention' (ASV, JPS 1917). 12:5 qere participle as a wish, 'let this be known' (ASV, NJPS). 12:6 'O inhabitant of Zion' (ASV collective). Quotation marks: the first song runs 12:1b-2 and the second 12:4b-6, with 12:3 as narration between them (JPS 1917 and NJPS mark the same extents).
entries.rationale: Each item is a site where the Translator flagged a choice among standard renderings. The Editor keeps the Masoretic text and the ASV baseline unless the corpus's concordance rules require a change, and records the alternatives. (1) The short form yāšōḇ and the non-consecutive ûṯᵉnaḥămēnî, if pressed, give a wish. ASV, JPS 1917 and NJPS read a statement, which suits a thanksgiving (ʾôḏᵉḵā), and the Vulgate also has a past statement (recalled; the LXX was not verified). The Translator's report that the versions read a wish is therefore not followed. (2) ʾēl has the same form in the absolute and the construct. The nominal clause (ASV, JPS 1917) is kept, and NJPS's construct is noted. (3) maʿyān is a spring or fountain (BDB; HALOT), but 'wells' is the established English of the verse and matches šāʾaḇ 'draw water'. The central maʿyān entry (Gen 7:11 'fountains of the great deep') is cosmic in scope and is not extended. (4) 12:4a repeats Ps 105:1 = 1 Chr 16:8 word for word, and the line follows ASV's wording of the psalm. qārāʾ bᵉšēm is the invocation formula governed by central qara-b-shem-yhwh. The 'proclaim' sense (JPS 1917, NJPS; cf. Exod 34:5) is recorded. When psalms-woh 105 or a Chronicles translation is drafted, a central parallel entry on the model of isa-2-2-4-mic-4-1-3-zion-pilgrimage-parallel-cross-corpus is recommended. (5) mûḏaʿaṯ is a participle (the qere; the ketiv is the Pual form). It is read as a wish after the imperative, with ASV and NJPS, and JPS 1917's statement is noted. (6) yôšeḇeṯ + place name is the idiom for a town's population (Mic 1:11-13), so the ASV collective is kept, and the enthroned-city reading is noted. None of these choices carries a lens.
